title: In their own Words: Why Low-Income Adults in Nairobi Adopted Mobile Money

detail.abstract: Survey research on technology adoption usually measures social and cultural influence with rating scales written by researchers. This paper asks what people say when they explain adoption in their own words. In a survey of low-income adults in three informal settlements in Nairobi, Kenya, 95 respondents answered an open question about the cultural reasons for their adoption of mobile financial services. We coded the answers by content analysis and compared them with the same respondents’ answers to rating-scale items and their reported use. Two-thirds of the answers (65%) attributed adoption to social pull: the influence of peers, neighbours, family and the sense that “all the people I know use mobile money”. Smaller groups described obligations and exchange within networks of kin and community (18%), a wish not to be left behind by technology (13%), the absence of cultural barriers (6%) and constraints of access (4%). Several older respondents said their children had persuaded them to adopt. Respondents whose answers expressed social pull scored higher on the social influence scale, and those who described obligations scored lower, supporting the validity of both measures. Stated reasons for adoption were not clearly related to how often respondents used mobile money. The findings give voice to the quantitative finding that social influence drives adoption, and suggest that the reasons people give for starting say little about whether they stay.

detail.abstract: Failure of applied Reinforcement Learning (RL) to solve a given problem predominantly stems from unaddressed "specification gaps," where the intent of human experts in the problem's domain is inaccurately or incompletely translated by AI into mathematical objectives, constraints, and reward functions. Failure can also stem from unaddressed "performance gaps," where human domain experts are unable to determine the validity of the RL based solution or where parameters (i.e., hyperparameters or weights on the reward terms comprising the reward) are poorly chosen. Chat Assisted Reinforcement Learning (CARL) bridges these gaps through a human-AI co-design interface architecture that enforces interactive specification prior to code generation and then enables subsequent verification and parameter alterations via iteration. More specifically, CARL leads domain experts through a structured ten-step workflow for each iteration using step-specific skill files, domain-aware suggestions via an assistant persona (called Trillian), and compact decision summaries that maintain context across iterations without context overload. Once the domain expert confirms the Markov decision process (MDP) specified by this procedure, CARL's autonomous tool-use loop generates, tests, executes, and debugs an end-to-end RL training pipeline, followed by an interactive post-training diagnosis and revisit step that allows for verification and parameter alteration before running a new iteration if desired. We apply CARL to two disparate, path-dependent optimization domains: (1) goals-based wealth management in finance and (2) dynamic-pressure-constrained Goddard rocket control in aerospace engineering. In both of these examples, CARL demonstrates that interactive specification engineering using human domain expertise throughout the process resolves critical failure modes (such as reward hacking and state aliasing) and consistently produces viable policies where unguided, fully autonomous code generation fails. Full implementation available at https://github.com/srdas/carl.

detail.abstract:
A production outage is more than a technical interruption. It is a business event that consumes engineering hours, delays customers, creates operational uncertainty, increases support volume, and exposes weaknesses in the organization’s prevention, detection, response, escalation, and learning systems. The most expensive incidents are not always the longest. They are often the incidents in which the organization loses time determining who owns the problem, which evidence is trustworthy, whether the preventive controls actually worked, and how to obtain timely assistance from a product vendor.
This paper examines a recurring scenario: production becomes unavailable or materially degraded even though preventive measures were supposedly in place. Internal technology staff spend hours troubleshooting. A ticket is opened with product support, but the product team responds slowly or provides low-confidence guidance. Meanwhile, the organization continues to lose money through service disruption, delayed transactions, manual workarounds, overtime, customer remediation, and management attention.

detail.abstract: Evidence scope: The empirical evidence comprises independently evaluated network-flow classification and system-log anomaly detection. The datasets do not contain a verified shared asset-level event timeline; consequently, no paired multimodal fusion score, GPU-specific failure forecast, hardware-to-attack causal effect, or production external-validation result is claimed. The proposed fusion architecture is a design contribution pending incident-linked prospective evaluation. Enterprise computing failures and cyber intrusions can share observable symptoms, including elevated resource demand, unusual traffic, and anomalous system logs. This study develops an explainability-oriented architecture for analyzing these signals without conflating failure diagnosis with intrusion attribution. We perform a fresh, reproducible experiment on the NF-UNSW-NB15 NetFlow v1 corpus (1,623,118 flows) and a separate descriptive assessment of 2,000 structured BGL system-log entries. The security experiment compares class-balanced logistic regression and a 90-tree random forest on a seeded 120,000-record training sample and a disjoint 40,000-record test sample selected after stratified partitioning. The forest achieved 98.525% accuracy, 76.40% precision, 96.32% recall, 85.21% F1, 0.9977 ROC-AUC, and 0.9466 average precision; logistic regression achieved 60.595% accuracy, 9.18% precision, 89.12% recall, 16.64% F1, 0.8651 ROC-AUC, and 0.3561 average precision. The BGL sample contained 143 labeled anomalous lines and 1,857 normal lines. These results demonstrate source-specific anomaly evidence but not validated hardware-induced intrusion causality: the datasets originate from different systems and lack aligned machine identifiers, clocks, and confirmed cross-domain incident labels. The paper therefore distinguishes observed performance from proposed multimodal correlation, discusses explanations and leakage risks, and specifies the evidence required for future deployment.

detail.abstract: Financial inclusion statistics count accounts, and digital inclusion statistics count phones. Neither shows whether the poor use mobile money regularly, or how the way they reach a phone shapes that use. This paper uses survey data from 381 low-income adults in three informal settlements in Nairobi, Kenya, to compare three modes of phone access: owning a phone used by no one else (71%), owning a phone shared with others (20%) and having no phone at all (9%). Sharing was strongly concentrated among the least educated: 31% of respondents with primary education shared their own phone, against 7% of university graduates. Registration for mobile money was high in all groups with a phone, but depth of use differed sharply. Of those who did not share, 44% used mobile money daily; of those who shared, 12%. After controlling for education, gender and age, sharers had about one-third the odds of more frequent use (odds ratio 0.34) and used mobile money for a narrower range of purposes; the differences held among registered users and with controls for settlement. Half of those without a phone still used mobile money, through others’ phones. The findings suggest that shared access widens reach but limits depth: it lets people start using mobile money but makes regular, wide-ranging use less likely. Measures of financial inclusion that count registrations or phone access miss this difference.

detail.abstract: Background: Portable eye tracking offers a practical opportunity to strengthen concussion detection by bringing quantitative neurological assessment closer to the athlete and the time of injury. Earlier recognition and removal from contact are especially important when an athlete may sustain further impacts before recovering from an initial concussion. Objective: To assess the clinical value of portable eye and head tracking, define its potential contribution to player protection in American football, and propose a pathway toward real-time field monitoring. Methods: We critically synthesized selected athlete studies, consensus guidance, FDA device records, and evidence on continued play and repeat concussion. Targeted searches were updated on October 2026. This is a narrative review and proposed research framework without new participant data. Evidence synthesis: FDA-cleared ocular assessment aids demonstrate that eye tracking has a clinical role in concussion evaluation. Portable systems can quantify visual tracking and related functional changes rapidly, complement symptoms and examination, and support repeat assessment near the field of play. Synchronized head measurements add context for interpreting gaze stabilization and eye-head coordination. Research associates delayed removal and insufficient recovery between injuries with adverse outcomes, providing a strong rationale for shortening the interval from possible injury to evaluation. Continuous wearable monitoring could extend this approach by identifying concerning changes during participation and prompting immediate clinical review. This extension requires validation under the motion, lighting, and task variability of live sport; accuracy varies across existing tests and populations. Conclusions: Portable eye tracking is a clinically relevant component of a proactive concussionassessment pathway and a promising foundation for real-time player monitoring. Its potential protective contribution is earlier recognition, timely removal, and informed follow-up that limits further contact during recovery. Validated device use can be integrated with multimodal clinical care while field-monitoring extensions are tested prospectively. Neither a normal eye-tracking result nor an automated alert independently determines return to sport or establishes CTE prevention.

detail.abstract: Enterprise organizations are adopting artificial intelligence, cloud computing, the Internet of Things (IoT), distributed-ledger technologies, and advanced analytics to improve operational capabilities and support digital transformation. Integrating these technologies into existing enterprise software is difficult because new capabilities must coexist with legacy applications, established data structures, security requirements, governance arrangements, and business processes. This paper develops a literature-informed architectural framework for organizing these integration decisions. Drawing on literature concerning enterprise architecture, digital transformation, cloud-native systems, microservices, technology governance, and interoperability, the paper synthesizes recurring challenges and proposes a seven-layer model: business and strategic objectives; enterprise architecture governance; integration and interoperability; emerging-technology capabilities; cloudnative architecture; infrastructure and deployment; and monitoring and continuous improvement. The synthesis identifies legacy integration, interoperability, architectural complexity, scalability, security, data management, governance, and organizational capability as interdependent concerns. The framework treats technology adoption as an enterprise-wide architectural change rather than an isolated implementation task. It is intended as a conceptual planning aid; it has not been empirically validated, and the manuscript does not claim that it produces measured improvements in performance or integration success. The paper concludes with practical implications and priorities for future evaluation through case studies, expert assessment, and empirical testing.

detail.abstract: In many developing economies, ordinary people are turning to cryptocurrency for reasons that have little to do with speculation: bank accounts are scarce, inflation erodes savings and sending money home is expensive. This paper asks whether that adoption is widening access to finance for the unbanked and supporting growth, or mainly exposing households with little protection to new risks. Drawing on a structured narrative review of twenty peer reviewed studies, policy reports and working papers, it connects the evidence on crypto use to the older literature on finance, inclusion and growth, and uses mobile money as a benchmark for what successful digital inclusion looks like. The review finds that crypto assets lower the cost of cross border transfers and offer some protection against currency weakness, yet they reach mostly people who are already connected to the internet and to some form of finance. Price volatility, fraud and weak consumer protection limit the gains for poorer users, and El Salvador's national experiment with Bitcoin as legal tender produced low and fading take up once a cash incentive was spent. Direct household evidence on crypto use in Africa and Asia remains thin. The paper concludes that crypto is best seen as a complement to mobile money and stable digital payments, and that its contribution to growth depends on regulation, digital infrastructure and financial literacy. It closes with policy lessons for emerging markets, with particular attention to Nigeria.

detail.abstract: Banks have spent decades building systems of correspondent accounts, clearing houses and reconciliation teams to move money and record ownership. Blockchain technology offers a different model, in which participants share a single ledger and settlement can happen almost at once. This paper examines how far that model is changing traditional banking and financial services, and where its limits lie. Drawing on a structured narrative review of twenty sources from finance, economics and information systems, it maps blockchain uses across five banking functions: payments, trade finance, securities settlement, identity and compliance, and lending. The review finds the clearest gains in cross border payments, trade finance and settlement, where shared records cut delay, cost and counterparty risk. Gains in lending and retail banking are smaller and more uncertain, since card networks and instant payment systems already serve most retail customers well. Barriers include scalability, legal uncertainty, governance of permissioned networks, and the risk that smart contracts and shared data make collusion easier. Decentralised finance adds a further challenge, offering bank like services without a clearly accountable operator. The paper argues that blockchain is reshaping the infrastructure behind banking more than the customer facing side, and that banks which treat it as a tool for shared market infrastructure are likely to gain most. It closes with implications for banks and regulators, including those in emerging markets such as Nigeria.

detail.abstract: Many enterprise generative AI initiatives stall between a successful pilot and dependable production use. Industry forecasts suggest that at least 30% of generative AI projects will be abandoned after proof of concept, and that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027. This paper argues that the gap is primarily a management and delivery problem rather than a model-capability problem, and proposes a practitioner framework for go-live decisions. The framework rests on a single organizing analogy, treating an AI system like a new hire, and translates it into seven readiness checks (value, ownership, data, evaluation, guardrails, operations and adoption), six hard stops that block launch regardless of overall score, an eight-part evidence pack, a 0-2 scoring rubric, and an additional control set for agentic systems that can take actions. The checks are mapped to established sources including the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, the EU AI Act, and empirical work on machine learning engineering. Seven publicly documented cases are used to illustrate the failure modes each check is designed to catch. The paper closes with limitations and a proposed agenda for empirical validation.

title: Dilated Attention U-Net for Thyroid Nodule Segmentation in Ultrasound Images

detail.title: Dilated Attention U-Net for Thyroid Nodule Segmentation in Ultrasound Images

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no competing interests

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: Accurate delineation of thyroid nodules in ultrasound images is a prerequisite for reliable computer-aided diagnosis, yet it is complicated by speckle noise, low lesion-to-background contrast, blurred boundaries, and variability of nodule size and shape. We present the Dilated Attention U-Net (DA U-Net), a U-shaped encoder–decoder architecture that couples dilated convolutions and additive attention gating with residual dilated blocks, an atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASPP) bottleneck, and deep supervision. Twelve baselines spanning CNN, transformer, and Kolmogorov–Arnold families were retrained from scratch under strictly identical conditions on TN3K (2,303/576/614) and Thyroid/tg3k (2,868/358/359), and evaluated with region- and boundary-based metrics, paired significance testing, size-stratified analysis, and cross-dataset testing. On TN3K, DA U-Net attains the highest recall and F2 with Dice 0.8086, statistically tied with the strongest baseline and ahead of seven of twelve competitors (Holm–Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon). On Thyroid/tg3k it ranks first in Dice (0.9516) and ASSD (1.42 px), with the second-lowest HD95 (5.15 px). In a single-seed ablation, removing the dilated convolutions or the attention gates costs 16.1 and 7.8 Dice points on Thyroid/tg3k, whereas on TN3K no single removal changes Dice by more than ±1.2 points; removing deep supervision lowers recall on both datasets. A zero-shot cross-dataset experiment yields near-zero Dice in both directions, documenting a near-complete loss of transfer whose causes are not disentangled here, and providing a negative baseline for future domain-adaptation research. Under the evaluated protocols, DA U-Net shows the sensitivity-oriented behaviour desirable in segmentation backbone for thyroid ultrasound; its clinical value remains to be established.

detail.abstract: Background and Objective: Pump-failure death (PFD) and sudden cardiac death (SCD) in heart failure call for different decisions, but most risk tools predict all-cause mortality. We developed a competing-risk model for 4-year PFD, compared it with artificial intelligence (AI) methods, tested whether ECG/Holter data add value, and provide an open-source evaluation pipeline.,Methods: All 992 ambulatory patients of the multicentre MUSIC cohort were analysed, with SCD, non-cardiac death and transplantation as competing events. An 8-variable cause-specific Cox model was compared with Fine–Gray, elastic-net and gradient-boosting models using 50 × 5-fold cross-validation with fold-wise multiple imputation. Calibration, time-dependent AUC, net benefit, sensitivity, specificity and precision were estimated with competing-risk methods implemented in Python.,Results: Within 4 years, 104 patients (10.6%) had PFD. The 8-variable model was well calibrated (observed/expected 1.01; slope 0.90) with AUC 0.761 (95% CI 0.721–0.809). At a 10% threshold, sensitivity was 77%, specificity 67% and precision 21%, with net benefit 0.048 versus 0.007 for treating all. The elastic net performed equivalently (ΔAUC +0.005, -0.015 to 0.026); gradient boosting was worse (ΔAUC -0.036, -0.066 to -0.006). ECG/Holter data did not improve prediction (ΔAUC -0.003, -0.019 to 0.012). Calibration held across subgroups.,Conclusions: A parsimonious competing-risk model provides well-calibrated, clinically useful PFD risk estimates; AI methods and ECG data added no value. The open-source pipeline supports leakage-free evaluation of competing-risk prediction models.

detail.abstract: Geopolitical shocks can make finished fuels scarce even where crude remains available. This paper examines how the 2026 Iran war affected refined-product premiums and the role of alternative supply, using U.S. and northwest European prices, Hormuz shipping activity, inventories, refinery operations, and U.S. exports. A framework with joint production, storage, and costly spatial arbitrage links three questions: where products repriced, what limited replacement production, and how regional price signals were connected to trade. Event estimates show crack-spreads increase across refined petroleum products. Another evidence of downstream disruption is the association of the larger increases in crack spreads with the greater prewar refined products import dependence. Monthly interactions are consistent with inventories buffering disruption and high refinery utilization amplifying it, while lower Hormuz traffic is associated with wider diesel and jet-fuel cracks. Toda-Yamamoto tests reveal product-specific predictive links between regional price gaps and total U.S. exports: wartime diesel exhibits bidirectional predictability, jet-fuel exports predict the regional gap, and gasoline shows no significant link in either direction. These results connect downstream scarcity with international adjustment without interpreting predictive relationships as structural demand responses. Energy resilience depends on the ability to convert, store, and deliver fuel, as well as on access to crude.

detail.abstract: Objective. Proactive care programs require health systems to prioritize patients when outreach capacity is limited, yet risk-only tools may not capture clinicians’ trade-offs among risk, actionability, care gaps, and expected benefit. We evaluated whether pairwise preference learning can support label-efficient patient prioritization in a controlled simulation setting with complete reference rankings. Materials and Methods. A synthetic cohort of 1,000 adults was generated with age, a cardiovascular-risk proxy, and 16 binary actionable care-gap indicators. Ten clinician-inspired preference simulators produced pairwise labels reflecting diverse prioritization policies. RankNet, XGBoost, and logistic regression were trained under fixed pair sampling and active learning; a risk-only ranking served as a clinical baseline. Performance was evaluated on held-out patients using pairwise area under the curve (AUC) and top-of-list metrics. Results. Performance improved rapidly and plateaued after approximately 400 labeled comparisons. RankNet performed best overall. At 400 labeled pairs, RankNet with systematic fixed sampling achieved AUC 0.88 and normalized discounted cumulative gain at 20 (NDCG@20) 0.93. Replacing fixed sampling with active learning (Top-of-List Margin Refinement) improved head-of-list fidelity, increasing mean average precision at 20 (MAP@20) from 0.45 to 0.64 and rank-biased overlap (RBO) from 0.48 to 0.64, with AUC decreasing from 0.88 to 0.84. Learned rankings outperformed the risk-only baseline, and an exploratory large-language-model robustness extension preserved the same cross-model ordering. Conclusion. Pairwise preference learning recovered heterogeneous prioritization policies from limited pairwise supervision, while top-focused active learning improved fidelity at the head of the ranking.

detail.abstract: This paper examines some of the ways Final Fantasy Type-0 talks about death and grief during wartime through the difference between what characters know inside the game world and what the player knows outside it. The research question focuses on how this difference affects the way death and loss are experienced. To answer this, the paper compares Final Fantasy Type-0 with Final Fantasy VII, focusing on the deaths of Kurasame Kirigaya and Aerith Gainsborough. Through an analysis of specific scenes and research on grief, collective memory, and the treatment of military sacrifice, the paper examines how the two games handle the knowledge of death. In Final Fantasy VII, both the characters and the player remember Aerith, allowing them to share their grief. In Final Fantasy Type-0, the people of Orience forget those who die, while the player continues to remember them. Nine's and Kazusa's unexplained sense of emptiness after losing their mentor/friend suggests that forgetting does not necessarily remove grief. Instead, it can leave people unable to understand their own loss. The paper argues that Final Fantasy Type-0 uses this difference in knowledge to show how forgetting can hide the human cost of war, leaving the player as the only witness to the dead. This demonstrates how games can use the relationship between the player and the game world to explore death and grief beyond the events of the story itself.

detail.abstract: In August 2026, in a civil suit brought by a rural bank (bank perkreditan rakyat) in Sidoarjo, Indonesia, the defendants' counsel cited three Supreme Court (Mahkamah Agung) decisions by docket number and asserted that all three were "one hundred percent identical" to the case at hand, standing for the rule that a bank which does not restructure its debtor has defaulted and may not execute the collateral. The three numbers are genuine. Yet when the decisions were opened, none concerned banking: two were inheritance-land disputes and one a bankruptcy matter decided on the court's jurisdiction. This article reports that specimen, found through a sweep whose plan was preregistered and publicly frozen-on the Open Science Framework (osf.io/5gwej)-before any decision was read. It distinguishes three ways a judicial citation can mislead: fictitious (the number points to nothing), misplaced (the number is real but the attributed rule is not what was decided), and unexaminable (the source cannot be opened at any public door). The Sidoarjo citations are of the second kind, which survives a first-pass search precisely because the number resolves. The article keeps two honest limits: the citations sat in a party's argument and were not adopted by the bench, which decided the case on other grounds; and the inference of a machine behind them is drawn from pattern, not proof. It argues that the remedy is not detecting machines-often impossible from within the file-but restoring examinability: that nothing should ground a legal conclusion before it can be, and has been, opened.

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Factor of Production Fees Royalties and the Case for a Universal AI Dividend

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly purchased as a capability that performs cognitive tasks, yet its treatment in production analysis and income distribution remains contested. This conceptual article argues for recognizing deployed AI services as a separately measured productive input and for describing their contractual compensation as access fees or licensing royalties. It distinguishes this analytical proposal from the stronger claim that AI constitutes a primary factor irreducible to intangible capital. An integrative review connects task-based automation, intangible investment, information economics, technology licensing, and social dividends. A producer-provider framework separates the purchaser's AI expenditure from the provider's operating costs, normal returns, and economic profit, showing why gross fees cannot simply be added to national income as a fifth distributive share. The article then develops a normative case for sharing AI-related surplus with the public, grounded in collective knowledge contributions and publicly supported institutions. A universal AI dividend is proposed as a policy option alongside direct contributor payments and public investment. Such a dividend would require an explicit revenue base, cross-border allocation rules, and safeguards for innovation and privacy; its ability to finance a sufficient basic income cannot be presumed. The contribution is a framework linking AI input measurement, contractual remuneration, and collective benefit sharing without conflating their economic or ethical foundations.

detail.abstract: Empirical measures of adverse selection value a trade's information content by the move in the midquote over a fixed horizon after the trade. Five minutes is the convention. The SEC's 2024 amendments to Rule 605 now mandate horizons from 50 milliseconds to five minutes. Because the efficient price is latent, no horizon has been validated against the quantity it stands for. I validate it in a market where that quantity is observed: binary event contracts on Kalshi settle at exactly $1 or $0. Using minute-level quotes and exchange-recorded trade direction for 250,607 independently sampled events, I find that outside sports the five-minute midquote captures 68.7% of the price impact that settlement eventually reveals in the average market. The shortfall is governed by trading activity. The proxy captures under half of the information content of trades in the least active fifth of markets and overshoots by about a sixth in the most active. In thin markets more than a quarter of trades are followed by a midquote that has not moved five minutes later. Mispricing and momentum trading do not account for the pattern. The error also changes conclusions. The five-minute measure ranks markets whose outcome is known to a single person or company above broad-based markets in adverse selection, as a recent study of this exchange finds with other measures. Settlement reverses the ranking: the extra price impact in single-name markets is optimistic order flow that moves prices, persists at every observable horizon and carries no information about the outcome. Price impact that never reverses need not be information.

detail.abstract: One source of economic rents-preferential access to foreign currency through administrative allocation-was eliminated when Uzbekistan harmonized its official and parallel exchange rates in September 2017. This study looks at how, between 2013 and 2019, enterprises' performance, perceived corruption barriers, foreign currency borrowing, and access to financing evolved in Uzbekistan in comparison to Kazakhstan. It also considers the potential implications of these modifications on the redistribution of economic rents. This study estimates a comparative difference-indifferences (DiD-style) model using 3,675 firm-wave observations from the 2013 and 2019 World Bank Enterprise Surveys, using Kazakhstan as the comparator nation. Businesses in Uzbekistan do not exhibit a statistically significant shift in perceived barriers to financing when compared to Kazakhstan. Although this conclusion is not resilient to survey weighting, there is a modest decrease in the likelihood of carrying a loan. The likelihood that the most recent loan being made in foreign currency rises among businesses that have loans. Businesses also report weaker nominal sales growth and greater perceived corruption barriers. Since the three-wave checks using the 2008/09 data deny parallel pre-trends for several outcomes, the results should be viewed as descriptive rather than causative. The most constant result across all specifications is the rise in the perceived corruption-obstacle score. The results do not explicitly prove that rent-seeking possibilities were reduced, but they are compatible with the idea that they were redistributed.

detail.abstract: Root cause inference for nuclear power plant equipment failures requires synthesizing causal information dispersed across multiple failure event reports, yet existing extraction methods produce isolated cause-effect pairs that lack the connectivity needed for systemlevel reasoning. This paper proposes a framework that constructs causal graphs from nuclear licensee event reports using a fine-tuned large language model, and performs root cause inference over the resulting graph structure. The framework operates in two phases. In the graph construction phase, a fine-tuned LLM extracts cause-effect pairs from event report narratives, and these pairs are aggregated into a directed causal graph in which nodes represent failure events or equipment states and edges represent causal relations. In the inference phase, a path-based reasoning algorithm identifies candidate root causes by tracing backward through the causal graph from observed failure symptoms, ranking candidates by path strength and frequency across reports. We evaluate the framework on a corpus of United States nuclear power plant failure event reports, comparing graph-based inference against flat pair-level extraction and against retrieval-augmented LLM prompting without graph structure. Results show that causal graph construction enables the identification of multi-step failure pathways that pairlevel methods cannot capture, and that root cause candidates ranked by graph-based inference align more closely with expert-identified root causes than candidates produced by non-graph baselines. The framework addresses a critical gap between causality extraction and actionable failure analysis, offering a structured representation that supports downstream reliability and risk assessment activities.

detail.abstract: This essay asserts that the use of artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled mass surveillance and data processing strategies, tools, tactics, techniques, and procedures (“TTP”) by competing domestic and foreign militaries, intelligence agencies, and non-state threat groups places special and unanticipated burdens on civic relationships, liberty interests, as well as other constitutional doctrines, that are inconsistent with the Framers’ intent for the security services the national government was to provide. America’s time-honored written Constitution, as well as America’s less stable but often powerful constitutional institutions and culture, places America’s citizens in a better and perhaps unique position to resist high tech mass surveillance and to preserve meaningful popular sovereignty. However, America’s open democratic society and legacy culture of popular sovereignty also create special vulnerabilities to subversion by enemies foreign and domestic. First, we will establish some propositions that help to define and contextualize America’s legacy constitutional framework and aspirational culture of popular sovereignty from the perspective of a security mindset. We will then describe part of the fact pattern of contemporary AI-powered mass surveillance and data processing technology employed by the military and intelligence world and evaluate the burdens it places on constitutional rights, duties, and relationships. Finally, we will tie it all together with some concluding remarks and express aspirations for a new defense of constitutional republicanism.

detail.abstract: Event-management research has long stressed planning, risk assessment, and contingency planning. Much less has been written about how producers make decisions in real time when a plan fails on the day of an event. This paper combines established event-management and organizational-resilience literature with reflective practice from nearly two decades of producing concerts, festivals, and private and corporate events. It proposes a four-part framework for operational resilience in live production: anticipation, redundancy, coordination, and continuity. A 2019 case of transport failure on the day of a performance illustrates the framework. detail.abstract: Organisational diagnosis requires judgements about internal conditions, their relationship to an intended purpose and their effects on collective functioning. This paper presents the Internal Context Map, an instrument for assessing whether an organisation’s internal conditions support a stated mission or vision. The map examines four dimensions: governance, resources and capabilities, culture, and leadership and power. Each dimension is assessed through a guiding question, observable indicators, supporting evidence, identified gaps and an ordered qualitative position. Collective functioning is assessed separately along a continuum from fragmented to collaborative and compared with the dimensional findings. The paper examines three design choices: an explicit reference for judgement, a documented sequence from evidence to assessment, and a separate examination of collective functioning. It positions these choices alongside four established organisational diagnostic models and explains how discrepancies between assessments can guide further enquiry. The proposed contribution concerns the organisation and interpretation of diagnostic judgements. The paper presents no empirical findings on reliability, validity or organisational outcomes. It identifies priorities for independent assessment, comparative case research and evaluation against established approaches.

detail.abstract: A hedger can keep a fixed hedge ratio current in two ways, by re-estimating it all the time or by watching it and refitting when a monitor signals a change. The second is the natural answer to structural change. On daily hedges since 1930 we find that it does not pay. Over 428 four-year blocks of 39 relationships, under a design fixed before any loss was computed (two of its 41 relationships are omitted here for licensing reasons), monitoring costs 0.049 of the frozen hedge's loss against a 250-day rolling window, three times the window's own estimation cost. The ranking holds in all five further samples fixed before their data were downloaded (1,407 relationship-blocks), significantly in four. Neither the monitor nor its fastest form beats the best of rolling windows, a tuned discount and a two-component Kalman filter in any of 21 families. A monitor, we argue, is a window that stops and restarts. While it waits for evidence its hedge goes stale, and its alarms find the right periods but not the right days. Each refit then restarts the estimate, which pays only if the slope drifts faster than these slopes do over a year or more. A faster monitor narrows the gap without closing it, and even exchange-rate regime changes dated by monetary history favour the window.

While these technology opens a far superior ways for them to learn, it also intensified the predominance of cyberbullying making it one of the most problematic concerns of Philippine education. Cyberbullying is the repeated way of harassment, threats embarrassment of people using digital devices, platforms and computer applications. Unlike traditional bullying this type of bullying is hard to control as it occurs anonymously and can spread quickly across the digital world. Additionally, it gives psychological and emotional damage to victims that often result in depression, anxiety or even suicide. In recent report of UNICEP, about 43-44% of Filipino learners are victim of this deadly cyber bullying which corrupted their young minds and affect their academic performance. This narrative review examines the existing educational policy framework that addresses the growing problem of cyberbullying in the Philippines. Specifically, it analyzes the provision, implementation, strength and limitation of the existing laws and DepEd policies such as Republic act 10627 or Anti-Bullying act of 2013, Republic act 10175 or Cybercrime prevention act of 2012, Republic act 10173 or Data privacy act of 2012 and applicable DepEd issuance on child protection and anti-bullying. This review article combines current evidences came from government documentation, and policy reports regarding the effectiveness of various policies in protecting learners from online harassment.
Persistent challenges ware shown in the process of analysis, these includes inconsistent policy implementation, inadequate preparedness for teachers and parents, underreporting of cyberbullying incidents, low digital literacy and the absence of school based monitoring and intervention mechanism. Furthermore, the review highlights the need for stronger collaboration among school stakeholders, better digital literacy programs and updated policy guidelines that address a more complicated cyberbullying due to evolving digital technologies. By examining the current law and policy landscape, this narrative review may provide support to policy makers, educators and school administrators in strengthening legal protections against the problem of cyberbullying. It may also help in creating better educational strategies that promotes safer digital learning environment for Filipino learners.

detail.abstract: Launching a drone from a traditional delivery vehicle to serve one or more customers before returning to the truck creates numerous planning challenges related to synchronizing drone routing with truck routing. One flexible and versatile approach to addressing these challenges is through the use of "operations" as a structural framework. An operation models the complete route cycle from the moment a drone departs from the truck until it returns, while the truck simultaneously serves one or more customers during this period. Since each operation represents only a small subproblem, various practical restrictions and constraints can be easily incorporated into the model. In this chapter, we examine the advantages and limitations of this structure, and discuss several problem features that can be modeled in this structure.

detail.abstract:
Organizations constantly manage complexity by substituting observable indicators for unobservable constructs. This conceptual paper introduces a governance framework explaining how informational decision aids evolve into unexamined administrative gates, termed governing proxies. At its operational core, a governing proxy is defined by its function as a filtering mechanism that separates a subset from a larger population to control access to opportunity, capital, prestige, or fuller evaluation. 

We decouple two properties routinely conflated in management and organizational literature: Gatekeeping Power (G), the structural authority an indicator exercises over access, and Signal Validity (V), its context-specific empirical accuracy relative to the underlying construct. We formalize a dynamic continuum culminating in Power-Validity Divergence (ΔG > ΔV). We argue that this breakdown does not require malice, deception, or intentional metric gaming. Instead, it is driven by Coupled Rationality across expanding institutional networks. 

Integrating classical signaling theory (Spence, 1973; Kirmani & Rao, 2000), we demonstrate that universal automated screening collapses the non-signaling alternative to near zero (D → 0), structurally forcing a pooling equilibrium (C > D) where all candidates must acquire the proxy badge regardless of aptitude. We show that self-correction fails due to Verification Masking, where downstream direct evaluation successes are misattributed to upstream filters while the excluded counterfactual pool remains unobserved. We analyze cross-domain applications in hiring, professional social platforms, and academic publishing, offering actionable interventions including the Proportionality Principle, the Alternative-Pathway Test, and Proxy Review Boards.
Declaration: Generative AI was used for editorial assistance and drafting synthesis. Conceptual formulation, core theory, and assertions are the original work of the author.

detail.abstract: Social ventures diversify revenue to secure resources for their missions, yet diversification taxes the scarce attention and administrative capacity on which these organizations depend. We develop a theory of how artificial intelligence, conceived as an entrepreneurial actor rather than a passive tool, reshapes this trade-off. Integrating research on revenue diversification in social entrepreneurship with real options reasoning and the attentionbased view, we argue that AI agency enlarges the set of diversification opportunities a venture perceives, lowers the cost of coordinating multiple revenue streams, and converts diversification from a lumpy commitment into a portfolio of staged, reversible experiments. These same mechanisms create a distinctive hazard, algorithmic mission drift, in which optimization toward measurable revenue objectives crowds out attention to the social mission. The resulting relationship between AI-enabled diversification and social performance is curvilinear and depends on mission governance, on the task environment, and on the drive, political skill, and persistence of the entrepreneur. We further theorize that reliance on a single model homogenizes diversification choices across ventures. The framework yields eleven propositions and an agenda for research on AI in hybrid organizing.

detail.abstract: This article develops an integrated model of state governance of petroleum field development by reconstructing the Norwegian petroleum-governance experience and modernizing its decision architecture for international application. The authors interpret Norway's Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG), with assets of approximately USD 2.3 trillion at the stated 2026 reference date, as a long-term economic result of applying the Norwegian State Project Model. The research examines eight countries, nine legal regimes and sixteen petroleum projects. First, it reconstructs a Norwegian State Project Model encompassing integrated development planning, independent appraisal principles, public authorization, implementation oversight and the fiscal conversion of petroleum receipts into financial wealth. Second, it develops the authors' modernized Base Model, comprising BM1-Integrated Development Plan; BM2-independent QA1, QA2 and proposed QA3; BM3-State Approval Authority; and BM4-Integrated Governance Process. QA3 is proposed for independent reassessment of material post-approval changes. Third, a Hypothetical Norwegian State Project Model estimates the potential annual accumulation of petroleum wealth in seven comparator countries through adoption of arrangements analogous to the Norwegian State Project Model. Under an illustrative assumption of USD 30 per produced barrel, potential aggregate annual contributions to national petroleum funds amount to USD 498 billion per year. The Hypothetical Norwegian State Project Model demonstrates the potential for substantial annual petroleum wealth accumulation through arrangements analogous to the Norwegian State Project Model, without requiring the additional QA3 mechanism proposed in the modernized Base Model. The study distinguishes documented institutional practices from the authors' methodological contributions and identifies areas requiring further verification through primary project-level evidence.

detail.abstract: Hybrid and multi-cloud enterprise environments connect information across platforms with different interfaces, operational responsibilities, and policy mechanisms. Integration can improve access to distributed data while also propagating semantic inconsistencies, quality defects, and inappropriate permissions. This structured narrative review examines how intelligent integration mechanisms and organizational governance can be coordinated across these boundaries. Scholarly research on schema matching, semantic integration, distributed data processing, provenance, and governance is synthesized with authoritative cloud security guidance. Intelligence is treated as a range of rule-based, metadata-assisted, and algorithmic capabilities whose outputs require evidence proportionate to their consequences. The synthesis distinguishes technical connectivity from agreement about meaning and separates reusable governance requirements from provider-specific enforcement. Materialized, virtual, and event-driven integration offer different tradeoffs involving freshness, availability, duplication, and policy coverage; no approach is established as universally superior. An original, unvalidated integration assurance framework is proposed to connect use definition, mapping qualification, policy translation, controlled operation, and reassessment. The contribution is a decision-oriented account of how semantic and authorization assumptions can remain visible as data crosses enterprise boundaries. Evaluation should jointly assess meaningful output correctness, authorized usability, recovery, and operating costs. The framework supports prospective enterprise assessment without claiming experimental validation, autonomous semantic understanding, or guaranteed regulatory compliance.

detail.abstract: Training needs analysis (TNA) is often treated as a formality, so training risks being poorly targeted and having no impact on job performance. This article aims to outline a blueprint for designing learning that makes an impact, from TNA to the evaluation of performance impact. The study is a literature review of previous research and textbooks on human resource training and development. The discussion covers gap mapping and prioritization, the instructional design reaction chain from training need to performance result, the formulation of measurable outcomes using performance, condition, and criterion, the selection of competency types (conceptual, procedural, interpersonal, and judgement), understanding adult learners through work experience, digital literacy, and andragogical principles, the ADDIE framework, and learning transfer and performance impact evaluation using the Kirkpatrick model. The review indicates that training impact depends on the accuracy of needs analysis, the clarity of outcomes, the fit between design and participant characteristics, and work-environment support for learning transfer. Therefore, instructional designers need to set performance indicators from the analysis stage so that the impact of training can be demonstrated.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines how Canadian defamation law seeks to reconcile two fundamental and sometimes competing values: freedom of expression and the protection of reputation, dignity, and privacy. It compares the treatment of civil defamation in Quebec’s civil-law system with the common-law approach in English Canada, while also considering the continuing role of criminal defamatory libel and the development of anti-SLAPP legislation.

The paper argues that, despite doctrinal differences, both legal traditions pursue a common objective of balancing expressive freedom against the protection of individual reputation. It examines the distinctive Quebec approach, in which even truthful statements may in some circumstances attract liability where their publication is unreasonable, and contrasts this with the common-law framework and its emphasis on defences such as justification, fair comment, privilege, and responsible communication.

The paper then considers how anti-SLAPP legislation and constitutional values have shifted the balance toward freedom of expression, while potentially creating barriers for individuals seeking to vindicate reputational harm. It argues that criminal defamation should be reconsidered because of its chilling effect, while civil remedies should better address serious reputational and privacy harms. Particular attention is given to the digital environment, where online publication can magnify the persistence, reach, and personal consequences of reputational harm. The paper concludes that Canadian defamation law should continue to evolve toward a more coherent balance between expression, dignity, privacy, and meaningful access to remedies.

detail.abstract: This paper develops an endogenous growth model of debt sustainability under monetary-fiscal policy interaction. Fiscal policy follows a Bohn-type feedback rule, while monetary policy follows a growth-augmented Taylor rule. The model emphasizes how seigniorage links the inflation rate, the government-debt-to-output ratio, and the primary balance. The analysis shows that stronger fiscal feedback lowers the government-debt-to-output ratio and can shift the primary balance from surplus to deficit when the government-debt-to-output ratio falls below a threshold. Conversely, a lower inflation target or a higher perceived neutral real rate reduces inflation and seigniorage, thereby raising the government-debt-to-output ratio and requiring larger primary surpluses.

detail.abstract:
A house purchase is for many people the largest financial decision of their lives. Yet 15-30% of American homebuyers waive inspections. Lawmakers have sought to institute a no-waiver policy preventing this practice. I propose a tractable model where buyers with heterogeneous valuations and risk aversion make offers to a risk-averse seller. Each offer (i) specifies a price and (ii) either includes an inspection contingency or waives inspections. The house's repair cost is uncertain. It is shared between the winning buyer and the seller if the winning offer includes an inspection contingency. 

     I show that the prevalence of inspection waivers in a seller's market can be explained by limited buyer bargaining power to negotiate seller remediation after an inspection. Even so, the no-waiver policy distorts risk-sharing between the seller and the winning buyer, thereby tending to decrease welfare. However, it reduces inequality, benefiting less wealthy (and thus more risk-averse) buyers by softening the competition they face from wealthier (and thus more risk-tolerant) buyers who would otherwise waive inspections. The policy can increase welfare by inducing homeowners to maintain their homes more efficiently before selling them.

detail.abstract: Structural smoothing techniques like auxiliary income or taste shocks are widely used to resolve non-differentiable boundaries in discrete-continuous macroeconomic models, but they can distort economic predictions and introduce numerical instability. We propose a soft-to-hard (StH) reinforcement learning framework that solves the exact, unsmoothed economy. The algorithm initializes on a smoothed approximation but systematically anneals this smoothing to zero during training, enforcing exact hard-switch Bellman operators at convergence. We provide two complementary StH implementations: tabular Q-learning (StH-Q), which delivers high numerical precision in low-dimensional settings, and neural actor-critic (StH-AC), which ensures scalability in high-dimensional environments. Applied to a multi-period sovereign default model, StH recovers the exact equilibrium where permanent smoothing falters.

detail.abstract: Orthopedic implant supply chains face clinical response deadlines, intraoperative size uncertainty, and batch expiry constraints. Drawing on a management case from a Chinese manufacturer, we examine how information on actual consumption supports multi-echelon inventory decisions. The framework links inventory flow conservation, forecast consumption, batch action windows, and reservations for candidate sizes. A gamma-Poisson model with common demand shocks separates the penalty from dedicated partitioning across demand classes from spatial pooling benefits, incorporating holding and shrinkage costs by location and delivery charges. Integer enumeration and generalized Gauss-Laguerre quadrature are validated through simulations using common random numbers: 400,000 cycles in each of 27 demand scenarios, supplemented by 432 cost scenarios. At a 99% joint cycle service target, the hybrid policy reduces initial stock by 16.07% in the baseline scenario. Centralization that disregards urgent response deadlines yields a timely unit fill rate of approximately 80.00%. In a counterexample with low mean demand, dedicated hybrid pooling requires 2.50% more units but becomes less costly when the local cost premium exceeds a threshold adjusted for delivery charges. Against a randomized capacity benchmark, the Net Deterministic Grid Premium accounts for 5.356 units of the 23 units saved in a scenario with low demand and no urgent cases. Nested sharing in which urgent demands are settled first enlarges the feasible set by restoring access across demand classes. These findings identify trade-offs among stock quantity, local risk exposure, and delivery costs within a framework of Triple Decoupling and Dual Pooling. Extensions address the Elasticity of Inventory Substitution by Information, nonstationary basestock rules reflecting procurement quotas, controlled sterilization postponement, and release triggered by inventory events, alongside a design for evaluating phased implementation.

detail.abstract: AI customer service is usually judged by how many conversations the chatbot handles on its own and how quickly it replies. These numbers do not show whether the customer's problem was actually solved. A conversation can end smoothly while the problem stays open. This article proposes a framework for following an issue from the first chatbot message, through any handoff to a human agent, to a verified outcome. Unlike measures that look only at the end result, it shows where in the journey things went wrong. The framework has five dimensions: whether the AI is still making progress, whether and when the case should move to a person, whether key details carry over in the handoff, whether promised actions are completed, and whether the problem is fixed. I call this service continuity. Customer effort, wait time, and staffing capacity are tracked alongside as context. The article provides working definitions, an illustrative case, dashboard specifications, escalation logic, and a plan for testing it. The framework has not yet been empirically validated; Section 5.1 sets out how to test it.

detail.abstract: The enduring challenge in financial machine learning lies in the stochastic, non-stationary nature of asset price distributions, where the signal-to-noise ratio is notoriously low. Traditional monolithic trading algorithms, which attempt to simultaneously learn entry and exit logic within a single objective function, frequently suffer from overfitting to regime-specific noise and fail to account for the asymmetric nature of market liquidity and volatility. This research paper presents a rigorous, exhaustive evaluation of the Hunter-Guard strategy, a dualmodel architecture that decouples trade initiation ("Hunter") from trade liquidation ("Guard") using ensemble learning methods. Central to this framework is the novel and counterintuitive application of Synthetic Sentiment-the injection of uniform random noise as an input feature-which we posit functions not merely as data augmentation, but as a form of explicit regularization mathematically equivalent to Tikhonov regularization, effectively mitigating the narrative fallacy and algorithmic bias. Through a detailed dissection of the Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBR) implementation, portfolio correlation constraints, and advanced risk metricsspecifically achieving a Sortino Ratio of 3.86 and a Calmar Ratio of 3.4-we demonstrate that the decoupling of buy and sell decisions allows for the optimization of asymmetric risk-reward profiles. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical justification for noise injection, drawing parallels to stochastic resonance and "Noise Injection Node Regularization" (NINR), ultimately arguing that the Hunter-Guard paradigm offers a robust alternative to conventional sentiment-driven strategies that are vulnerable to concept drift and linguistic non-stationarity.

Delegated choice carries four costs that disclosure does not remove: an inaccurate representation of what the principal wants, weight given to parties who hold no mandate, preferences moved by what the agent buys, and lock-in to the agent that holds the representation. Disclosure reaches the second alone, and only where the agent’s rule acts on the label. This paper develops the fifth and last component of the Theory of Delegated Markets: the design of institutions that preserve the efficiency of delegated choice while controlling those costs. I define seven institutions and a disclosure baseline as measurable properties of a market: separable mandates, portable preference capital, the computational fiduciary, independent audit against a benchmark outside the agent, liability on the least-cost avoider, contestable consideration sets, and governed updates. Five boundary conditions are stated as premises. An accounting decomposition places each institution as an instrument that moves the Delegation Possibility Frontier, chooses a point 2 

on it, or measures where an architecture sits. Nine design propositions follow, DM1 to DM9, each with a mechanism, a boundary, and a falsifier; four institutional forms are compared; three designs are specified, none run. The construct is judged channel by channel: where disclosure alone closes more than one fifth of the gap to the direct-choice benchmark on the representation, endogeneity, or lock-in channel, the case for the institutions that act on that channel fails, and a failure on all three removes the case for the paper.

detail.abstract: Agentic AI can draft a persuasive answer in seconds. detail.abstract: PT Arina Shiva Group is a company engaged in providing innovative packaging products and modern business equipment to support culinary businesses of various sizes. This study aims to analyze the effects of performance appraisal and training on employee performance, with work ability serving as a mediating variable at PT Arina Shiva Group. Meanwhile, performance appraisal has a significant direct relationship with employee performance, although it does not demonstrate a significant effect on work ability. detail.abstract: The modernization of society has brought fundamental changes to Islamic religious outreach, affecting communication patterns, religious needs, and the relationship between religious counselors and communities. In this context, Islamic Religious Counselors face challenges arising from digital technological developments, the increasing diversity of socio-religious issues, demands for responsive public services, and the need to strengthen professional capacity. This article aims to critically analyze the challenges confronting Islamic Religious Counselors in the modern era, examine the transformation of their roles, and formulate strategies for strengthening professionalism. detail.abstract: Organizations use performance indicators to assess the achievement of goals, monitor processes, and inform decision-making. This article discusses how to establish meaningful success criteria as well as risks when organizations are too numerically oriented to indicators. detail.abstract: This study develops a country-level measure of the economic-industrial capacity of European NATO Allies to mobilise, replenish, maintain, and sustain military capability under strategic stress. The measure comprises four components: macroeconomic capacity, sectoral resilience, defence-industrial capability, and logistics and sustainment. The analysis covers 28 European Allies and evaluates a balanced baseline against five geoeconomic stress scenarios. The results distinguish baseline capacity from stress vulnerability and provide an assessment framework for identifying the economic-industrial bottlenecks that can constrain sustained military readiness. Baseline scores vary materially across countries, with a sample mean of 0.610 and a range from 0.471 to 0.759. The calibrated geoeconomic shocks reduce effective capacity in every scenario, though the effects are highly heterogeneous. The combined-stress scenario has the largest average effect, lowering the sample mean to 0.491, a decline of 19.5 per cent relative to baseline. TRS and PR operate mainly through defence-industrial and replenishment constraints; supply-chain fragmentation is driven primarily by sectoral exposure and substitutability; and external-support reduction operates through allied access and sustainment. Our results suggest shifting attention from expenditure targets alone towards the capacity to convert resources into usable military capability: the key issue is not only how much is spent, but also which bottlenecks limit the conversion of resources into capability.

detail.abstract:
This paper is the fourth in the series following “Attribution Space: A Missing Concept in HSE Theory,” “The Structural Compression of Attribution Space,” and “The Convergence Limit of Attribution Space.” The first three papers completed the conceptual definition, compression mechanisms, and limit boundaries of Attribution Space. The third paper pointed out that there is an irreducible minimum for the compression of Attribution Space, and that over-compression will push the system into an unpredictable “Overload State.”
This paper answers the core question left by the third paper: When Attribution Space is compressed to its limit by technological means, does it disappear? The core proposition is: Attribution Space splits into “Formal AS” and “Substantive AS.” Technological compression drives Formal AS toward zero, but simultaneously causes Substantive AS to approach infinity, resulting in a structural “Displacement.” This is not a simple spatial shift, but a “plastic phase transition” that occurs when the system crosses its elastic limit.
This paper constructs the “Human-Machine-Data Triangle” framework, systematically analyzing the accountability boundaries at three levels: (1) Human-Data interaction, leading to “the data didn't show it”; (2) Human-AI interaction, leading to confirmation fatigue (“the system didn't alert me”); (3) AI-Data interaction, leading to the responsibility gap (“the algorithm couldn't recognize it”). In this closed loop, responsibility is diluted with every rotation, ultimately resulting in the “hollowing out of the triangle” and the “inflation of exculpatory evidence.”
Based on this, the paper proposes the principle of “Meaningful Human Control” (MHC), supported by a positive validation from the aviation industry's FOQA mechanism. Finally, this paper warns highly traceable digital governance systems that accountability mechanisms must be elevated synchronously with compression mechanisms; otherwise, technological means will only accelerate the expansion of Substantive AS.

detail.abstract: Maintenance data quality influences both the credibility of failure predictions and the decisions those predictions support. However, improved classification performance does not establish that a maintenance policy is affordable, executable or economically preferable. This paper asks when improvements in maintenance data quality can change defensible policy choices under financial, staffing, skill and scheduling constraints. A focused critical review of twenty-seven scholarly sources is combined with a transparent symbolic decision analysis. The review connects work-order completeness, semantic consistency, temporal integrity and operating-context coverage with prediction validity and maintenance execution. The analysis separates uncertainty in failure probability from intervention cost, effectiveness and resource eligibility. For a simplified decision between maintenance and deferral over a defined horizon, it derives a break-even probability, a sufficient condition for decision stability and an upper bound on the loss from choosing the wrong action when probability error is bounded. These are conditional mathematical results rather than empirical estimates. The synthesis shows why corrective and scheduled preventive policies remain relevant where monitoring evidence is weak or response capacity is insufficient, while condition-based maintenance requires trustworthy observations and actionable warning. The distinct contribution is a decision-centred interpretation of data quality that links uncertainty to the margin between eligible alternatives. Practical implications concern targeted data improvement, protected technician time and validation against operational outcomes. No dataset, experiment, simulation or numerical performance improvement is claimed; prospective manufacturing studies are required to evaluate usefulness.

detail.abstract: Frontline employee empowerment in operational decision-making is often regarded as a means of improving service quality, but it also involves risks related to costs, inconsistency, and the misuse of authority. This article examines these issues through a real-world case: The Ritz-Carlton Hotel Company's policy of authorizing employees to resolve guest problems directly up to a specified monetary limit per guest per incident. Using a descriptive qualitative approach based on a singlecase study and a literature review, the case is analyzed through the stages of decision-making: problem identification, the development of alternatives, and alternative selection. The analysis indicates that bounded delegation, supported by training, information, shared values, and evaluation, has the potential to improve the speed and quality of service recovery. However, its primary risks include cost leakage, inconsistency, and poor decision-making. The most appropriate alternative is managed, bounded empowerment rather than centralized approval or unrestricted delegation. The evidence presented in this case is descriptive in nature and therefore requires further empirical investigation.

detail.abstract: Free societies ask citizens for small acts of affirmation. When does such a demand become a claim to say who is a good person? I call that claim moral jurisdiction, borrowing the vocabulary of jurisdiction as an analytical device. A Roman governor tested accused Christians with incense, a Qin minister proposed that students of the law take the officials as teachers, and a Christian schoolteacher in Tokyo hesitated before an imperial rescript on morals. I score the cases against three markers of a monopoly and argue that such a monopoly turns dissent into a defect of character and removes the dissenter's footing. Athens and Jerusalem each pointed to a standard outside the state, and Christian history supplied bodies that could hold it, though those bodies have knelt too. The line runs between orders that keep the standard and the standing outside the state and orders that do not, not between East and West. The evidence leaves non-Christian bodies, Plato and Aristotle, and the comparison with purely legal tyrannies untested (see also Yang 2026a).

detail.abstract: Autonomous and assisted driving have turned the automotive system-on-chip (SoC) into one of the most strategic components in a vehicle. This paper examines the market for autonomous-driving chips as of October 2026. It asks three questions: how growth in onboard AI workloads has reshaped demand for compute; how market structure is evolving between merchant suppliers and automaker in-house designs; and which constraints govern chip choice. Using company filings, industry installation data and secondary sources, we document a roughly hundredfold increase in fitted compute for comparable driving functions since about 2020. This increase is driven by end-to-end and vision-language-action (VLA) models with billions of parameters. In China, the largest market for advanced assisted driving, NVIDIA's share of domain-controller chip installations fell from 45.1% to 30.2% between early and August 2026, while Horizon Robotics rose from 9.3% to 19.8%. Leading Chinese automakers now ship their own 5nm and 4nm designs. A case study of NIO's Shenji NX9031 illustrates the economics of vertical integration: high fixed costs offset by per-vehicle savings and, increasingly, by external licensing. We interpret these developments through transaction-cost, property-rights and appropriability theory, and derive five propositions on when automakers make rather than buy driving chips. Chip choice is jointly constrained by cost, energy draw from the traction battery (5-15% of EV range), and new cybersecurity regulations (UN R155/R156; China's GB 44495-2024). We also map process nodes (from 8nm down to 2nm-class) and foundries, review US and Chinese export-control measures, describe the digital-twin and hardware-in-the-loop methods used to validate chips before installation, and compare published performance across five architecture types and seven L4 robotaxi operators, showing that peak TOPS is a weak predictor of real-world L4 safety. Finally, we map the upstream and downstream value chain, including optical data links and satellite positioning, where gross margins follow a smile curve: about 47-75% in chip design, against about 16-18% in integration and operations. We discuss implications for automakers, chip suppliers and policymakers.

detail.abstract: Studies that apply machine learning to financial forecasting often report that the importance of predictors changes over time and interpret this as evidence of structural change. We ask how much of such time variation can be distinguished from what models trained on noise would show, and how reliable the inference tools used for this purpose are. Using about 25 years of hourly bid and ask quotes for six currency pairs built from four currencies (EUR, USD, GBP, JPY), we train rollingwindow gradient-boosting classifiers of next-hour direction and summarise predictor importance with SHAP values aggregated into six groups. We compare the resulting series with those from up to 200 models trained on permuted labels per pair. Four results stand out. First, next-hour direction is weakly but persistently predictable (accuracy 51.2–52.0%), yet gross gains of 0.03–0.23 pips per trade are far below spreads. Second, part of the apparent predictability in the raw sample comes from the broker’s quotes around the daily rollover (23:00–02:00 Athens time) and disappears when those hours are excluded. Third, normal-approximation p-values for trend and break tests are liberal (rejection rates of 7–10% at a 5% nominal level), whereas empirical permutation p-values have correct size but need large null ensembles; power is about 35% for a three-percentage-point shift in an importance share and about 80% for a shift of eight to nine points. Fourth, with family-wise error control, no change in importance is statistically significant; the most consistent candidate, a 6-point decline in the weight of recent own-pair returns in EUR/USD alongside a fall in accuracy after 2015, has an adjusted p-value of 0.20 and weakens when only three independent exchange rates are used as features (p = 0.29); a logistic regression with the same inputs is about as accurate as the boosted trees. An extension to two further pairs, AUD/JPY and NZD/CAD (2015–2026, 200 permuted-label models each), gives accuracy of 50.9–51.2%, negative net results and no significant trend after adjustment. detail.abstract: I study whether a market maker quoting NIFTY and BANKNIFTY options (weekly and monthly expiries respectively) from a cloud server and a retail broker feed can survive informed order flow. Using my own five-level order book logs for 36 options per index (September 16 to October 23, 2026) and a replay with a queue model and NSE member costs, a quoter that joins the best bid and ask earns about Rs 12 (NIFTY) and Rs 23 (BANKNIFTY) of spread per lot per fill, pays about Rs 11 and Rs 18 in costs, and then loses Rs 32 and Rs 43 to the price move against it, nearly all of it within one second. In an oracle counterfactual that decides with the book of the same second, which no real system can do, the loss almost disappears: under the replay assumptions, timing accounts for most of the loss. Two signals predict bad fills: how far the index has moved since an option's quote last changed, and the probability of a stressed regime from a hidden Markov model trained on a year of earlier data. A strategy that pulls the threatened side and widens in stress was frozen before any test data were seen. On each of the complete test sessions so far, only four for NIFTY and three for BANKNIFTY, it lost less than the plain quoter: 46% less on NIFTY and 24% less on BANKNIFTY, in line with the development estimates of 40% and 20%. It still loses money, the evidence is too short to be statistically conclusive (sign test p = 0.06 and 0.125), and half of its NIFTY benefit disappears if its rules react one second late. The remaining losses come mostly from index jumps that reprice options within the same second. A follow-up rule that pulls all quotes after such jumps is pre-registered, with a placebo control, for evaluation on future sessions only.

detail.abstract: Institutions that adopt artificial intelligence do not only acquire a new tool; they acquire a new memory. Logs, case histories, training corpora, inferred profiles and retained outputs accumulate inside public bodies and decide, long after the original act, what the institution can say about a person. This article asks how the law should govern institutional memory when that memory is produced or processed by algorithmic systems. It uses the Brazilian novel O Prédio que Aprendeu a Escutar as an analytical object, not as evidence: the book imagines a courthouse whose records begin to write unsigned, uncontested entries about the inner lives of the people who work and litigate there, and then to resist being forgotten. Treated as a thought experiment, the narrative isolates five governance problems: memory without authorship, inference as exposure, entries without contestation, permanence as lock-in, and the human cost of maintaining the record. Each is tested against primary legal sources (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the GDPR, Brazil's LGPD, the Code of Civil Procedure and Resolution CNJ 615/2025) and against decisions and inquiries from the Court of Justice of the European Union, the Wisconsin Supreme Court, the Hague District Court and the Australian Robodebt Royal Commission. The article argues that traceability mandates and erasure limits are usually treated as opposing regimes, yet the novel shows that both fail when the record has no accountable author and no route to contestation. It derives five design propositions for public-sector AI records and states where the argument could be wrong. The analysis is interpretive, rests on a single literary text, and does not claim that any court operates as the novel describes.
