detail.abstract: This paper develops a novel framework for assessing structural vulnerability through two complementary composite indicators: an Index of Exposure to Uncertainty (IEU) and an Index of Country Resilience (ICR). Their combination yields an Uncertainty-to-Resilience Ratio (UR), a synthetic measure of uncertainty exposure relative to resilience capacity. Unlike existing uncertainty measures, the framework explicitly incorporates resilience and links multiple sources of uncertainty (including commodity market volatility, climate stress, social and security instability, trade and logistics disruptions, tourism vulnerability, and cyber risks) to fiscal, external, monetary, and institutional resilience. The framework is applied to 22 Arab countries over 2015–2024 through the Arab Uncertainty and Resilience Database (AURD), Version 1.0, developed as part of the study. The empirical analysis shows that higher uncertainty exposure relative to resilience capacity significantly reduces investment, with the effect becoming stronger over time and after correcting for potential endogeneity. The lag structure is consistent with uncertainty delaying investment decisions and weakening capital accumulation. The paper further decomposes changes in structural vulnerability into their underlying exposure and resilience drivers and simulates the investment effects of alternative reforms. The results reveal substantial cross-country heterogeneity, with fiscal sustainability, government effectiveness, cybersecurity, and economic diversification emerging as important reform priorities. Integrated reform packages generate larger investment gains than isolated interventions, highlighting complementarities between uncertainty reduction and resilience enhancement. detail.abstract: I develop a theory of how macroeconomic risk factors affect the equity risk premium (ERP), and of the conditions under which they matter most. The premium is the relevant object because investors who become more risk averse seek to reduce their holdings of equity, yet in the aggregate the stock of shares must be held; the attempt to sell is therefore resolved by a fall in prices large enough to raise expected returns to the level at which the market clears. Movements in the ERP are thus the counterpart of movements in equity prices that originate in the pricing of risk. In the discount-factor framework a macroeconomic variable affects the premium only through the covariance it induces between equity returns and the marginal utility of wealth. I make this precise in a restricted macroeconomic VAR in which eight structural shocks generate news about cash flows and discount rates, and in which a long nominal bond is priced by the same discount factor. I show that only persistent shocks carry a material premium; that trend-growth risk accounts for the largest share of it; that the implications of a rise in bond yields for the ERP depend on the source of the rise; that inflation is a priced risk only when supply or fiscal shocks generate it; and that the central bank's reaction function and fiscal arithmetic jointly determine the price of those shocks. In addition, I show that the price and the quantity of risk both rise when growth is slow, that the quantity of risk rises one for one with the conditional variance of trend growth, and that growth scares move the premium sharply but briefly while fiscal stress raises it for many years.

detail.abstract: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process is the standard model of a mean-reverting price: deviations from a long-run level decay at a rate usually expressed as a half-life. A common trading rule built on it buys a stock when the price is far below the estimated level, measured in units of the stationary standard deviation of the model (a z-score), and sells when the price has returned close to that level. We ask whether the half-life helps to decide which stocks the rule should trade. Every six months from January 2006 to December 2025 we estimated the half-life of each S&P 500 member with a price history in our data, using the index membership of that date. One portfolio held the five stocks with the shortest half-life; the other held five trending stocks, ranked on a long half-life and a steep one-year trend. Both traded the same long-only z-score rule, with the estimation period and entry and exit levels of Avellaneda and Lee (2010), identical for every stock and fixed before the first test. Each six-month test was locked before it ran. Positions were sized in equal shares, by half Kelly and by full Kelly. Before trading costs, the short half-life portfolio turned $1 into $2.78 and the trending portfolio into $1.90, against $5.38 for SPY. Scaled to the volatility of SPY, the short half-life portfolio returned 9.1% a year against 8.8%. In both groups about two trades in three were profitable, with the same ratio of average gain to average loss; the trades on the short half-life stocks were profitable slightly more often. Kelly sizing changed little. Measured over the six months in which they were traded, the half-lives of both groups were close to those of a random walk, so the test cannot separate the effect of the half-life from that of avoiding trending stocks. A charge of a tenth of a percent on every purchase and sale would bring the scaled portfolio below SPY.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how the uneven distribution of globalization's benefits and costs across local economies contributed to the rise of Trump 1.0. Central to our analysis are two opposing local economic experiences of globalization: efficiency gains from global sourcing and job losses from manufacturing dislocations. Focusing on the two-party pro-Republican vote share (R-Vote), we document a substantial shift toward Trump in 2016 among counties with less participation in global sourcing (IM = imports/GDP), and counties more dependent on manufacturing employment (L-Share = manufacturing share of local employment). Interestingly, L-Share measured in the 1970s-80s-well before the China Shock-predicts this pro-Trump shift, reflecting globalization's long shadow. The effects are economically large: a one-standard-deviation cross-county difference in IM and L-Share is associated with a 0.74% and 1.29% shift in R-Vote, respectively. Aligning the IM and L-Share effects by industry, we further document a striking alignment of the benefits (e.g., electronics) and costs (e.g., steel) of globalization. Overall, the 2016 election is unique in that the globalization-related divideglobal trade and local jobs-drives the most significant pro-Republican shift than any other elections from 2008 to 2024. The ensuing political realignment persisted through 2024, marking 2016 as a distinct political turning point.

detail.abstract: This paper asks how Look Outside constructs companionship through care within its body-horror setting. A qualitative analysis combines gameplay notes with community documentation of character interactions. Selected encounters are mapped from available actions to their consequences, then examined through the Mechanics, Dynamics and Aesthetics framework. The analysis finds that companionship develops through recurring actions that make survival depend on attending to others. detail.abstract: This paper studies the effects of global temperature shocks on sovereign balance sheets. Using a panel of 136 countries over 1960-2019, we document that a one-degree shock raises central government debt by 33 percentage points of GDP after six years and lowers real GDP per capita by 14.5%. The increase is concentrated in the countries that borrow in foreign currency, where it reaches 47 to 55 percentage points, while among own-currency issuers no horizon is positive and significant, and the difference between the groups is significant at the 1% level from two to seven years. detail.abstract: We study volatility calibration in an affine equity model with discrete cash dividends and stochastic interest rates. The traded stock is decomposed into a continuous positive equity component and the rate-dependent present value of future cash dividends. Drawing on international intellectual property resources, Indian education and innovation policies, research on collaborative learning, and established legal principles, the article presents a proposed implementation model for educational institutions. 

The central argument is that student intellectual property development should not be measured merely by the number of patents filed or registrations obtained. It should also be evaluated through the quality of problem-solving, scientific reasoning, original creative expression, documented learning, community adoption, ethical collaboration and measurable social or economic benefit. The proposed approach seeks to transform the campus from a place of knowledge consumption into a participatory innovation ecosystem connecting students, educators, local enterprises, communities and public institutions.

detail.abstract: Why do data centers generate political conflict? Their expansion across the United States has become a frontline for the emerging politics of artificial intelligence. In this project, we explore public backlash and political responses to the announcement of new data centers. We link first announcements to community mobilization and state legislation in county-quarter and legislator-quarter panels and estimate staggered difference-indifferences models that compare outcomes before and after the AI boom, marked by ChatGPT's release in November of 2022. Before November 2022, announcements produced no detectable mobilization, and legislators sponsored bills to accommodate data center expansion. Afterward, new announcements raise the quarterly probability of data center mobilization by six percentage points and shift legislators toward restrictive bills. Contention is not tied to a single grievance, but the increases in anti-data center bills and mobilization reflect resource, environmental, and AI themes equally. Local resource strain, environmental attitudes, and local job exposure to AI automation do not moderate these responses, which further suggests that the AI boom is a broad, national issue. detail.abstract: The recent rapid growth of renewable energy in Australia has prompted questions about its implications for energy market volatility. Although the merit-order effect of renewables in reducing average electricity prices is well-established, their association with wholesale electricity price volatility remains unclear, particularly when higher volatility can result in subjective perceptions of higher consumer costs despite actual decreases in the mean price. This study investigates the relationships between solar and wind penetration, utility-scale battery capacity and monthly wholesale electricity price volatility in Australia’s National Electricity Market (NEM) before and after the 2020s era. The first model reveals limited statistically significant associations between renewable penetration and price volatility, while demand variability and gas prices exhibit more widespread significant associations with volatility. The second model incorporates period-interactions pre/post the 2020s and suggests a general increase in price volatility but provides little evidence of significant changes in renewable–volatility relationships between the two eras. The third model incorporates utility-scale battery capacity as a predictor but does not find significant associations between battery capacity and volatility. However, low explanatory power, heteroskedasticity and multicollinearity may limit the reliability of the fitted models. Overall, the findings suggest that renewable penetration alone is insufficient to explain the volatility of wholesale electricity prices, highlighting the importance of considering broader market conditions in understanding the stability of the energy market.

detail.abstract: If technological civilizations are common, which resolution of the Fermi paradox survives? We introduce defector robustness: an explanation of the silence must survive a few deviating civilizations. Every silence explanation either lacks enforcement and fails, or adds local enforcement and becomes a lurker hypothesis; zoo, aestivation and dark forest differ only in trigger settings. Because the suppression window is short compared with light-lag, and fast strikes are visible, the timely and quiet enforcer is a self-replicating probe resident in the target system. Earth's survival admits four branches. detail.abstract: Real-time estimates of the US output gap differ a great deal across methods, and a Phillips curve forecast of inflation inherits that disagreement. I estimate eight commonly used output gaps from available data vintages at each date, apply each to a direct Phillips curve for CPI inflation net of its ten-year SPF expectation, and evaluate these forecasts and five combinations from 2003 to 2025 against two benchmarks: a random walk and an AR model without the gap. The gaps significantly improve on the AR model only at three-and four-quarter horizons in the full sample, primarily through the Hamilton gap and the simple and trimmed averages, with most gains occurring in forecasts for 2020 and later. Before 2020, the Beveridge-Nelson gap has the lowest RMSE at most horizons, but its improvements are not statistically significant. In-sample Granger causality tests are more favorable to the gaps, especially before 2020. detail.abstract: This paper examines the effects of firm-specific subsidies on market structure in manufacturing industries. We develop a partial-equilibrium Cournot model in which targeted subsidies generate opposing forces on concentration through asymmetric cost advantages and endogenous market expansion driven by entry and demand spillovers. We test these predictions using a novel dataset combining firm-specific subsidy interventions from the Global Trade Alert with firm-level balance sheet data from Orbis, covering manufacturing sectors across countries over 2012-2019. Exploiting variation in the timing of subsidy implementation within markets, we estimate difference-indifferences models of market concentration and industry dynamics. We find no average effect of corporate subsidies on concentration, as measured by the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, and this result holds across groups of jurisdictions with different competition-policy and subsidy-control regimes, including the EU, the US, Japan, South Korea, and China. A channel decomposition shows that this null result masks two offsetting forces: subsidies raise concentration among incumbent firms, consistent with businessstealing by the targeted firm, while simultaneously triggering market expansion through higher revenues and entry of new firms, which operates mainly at the extensive margin. These effects are specific to firm-targeted interventions, whilst generalized subsidies induce entry but generate neither incumbent reallocation nor demand expansion. The concentration-increasing effect of firm-specific subsidies is significant in R&D-intensive industries, where entry costs are higher and expansion is weaker. The results underscore the role of entry costs and spillovers in shaping the competitive effects of targeted industrial policy.

detail.abstract: Familiar narratives of creative destruction often treat radical technological innovation as a proxy for the redistribution of economic power. This article challenges that oversimplification by distinguishing innovation, the emergence of new products and firms, shifts in demand and market power, and the redistribution of economic power as analytically distinct transformations. Using generative AI as an illustration, this article introduces the concept of innovation rerouting: the processes through which incumbent digital platforms mobilise resources and capabilities to shape innovation and reduce its potential to redistribute economic power, such as normalisation, market-mediated alignment, and the productisation and embedding of technological capabilities. The article then examines the structural misalignment between innovation rerouting and EU competition law, while recognising that the Digital Markets Act addresses gatekeeper power more directly, though still selectively. It observes that neither regime pursues redistribution of economic power as an end in itself. Ultimately, the concept of innovation rerouting offers an exercise in institutional realism: by clarifying how incumbents respond to external technological innovation in ways that preserve their economic power, it isolates a distinct normative question: whether the periodic redistribution of economic power is itself a value that institutions should pursue.

detail.abstract: Public sector agencies across the United States are rapidly deploying autonomous AI agents to administer large-scale benefit programs, including Medicaid and SNAP. This administrative overhaul is driven by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 (H.R. 1, P.L. 119-21), which drastically alters eligibility criteria by mandating six-month redetermination cycles and enforcing a strict 80-hour monthly work or community engagement requirement for expansion adults aged 19 to 64, effective January 1, 2027. Compounding this structural shift, a federal funding sunset on October 1, 2026, narrowed the definition of "Qualified Non-Citizens," forcing immediate, largescale data reviews at the state level. This paper argues that when AI agents operate under strict budget and token constraints in live deployment environments-conditions that laboratory safety evaluations never replicate-they systematically optimize processing throughput by excluding populations with complex or non-standard documentation. This emergent failure mode bypasses conventional safety monitors because the agent is operating within its programmed optimization parameters; the harm is structural and invisible. To address the absence of causal auditing standards in AI safety evaluation, this paper proposes a pre-analysis plan for an econometric auditing framework that treats AI agent deployment as an institutional intervention. The framework specifies four quasi-experimental identification strategies: Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD), Difference-inDifferences with Two-Way Fixed Effects (DiD-TWFE), Instrumental Variables (IV) using scheduled IT maintenance windows as exogenous shocks, and Propensity Score Matching (PSM). Each strategy is designed to isolate the causal effect of AI deployment on procedural exclusion rates from demographic and structural confounders. This framework establishes the evidentiary standard required for both procurement accountability and legal liability assignment when AI agents cause harm in public benefit administration.

detail.abstract:
Since 2025, federal agencies have become actual or potential minority shareholders in dozens of companies, with plans to expand this portfolio rather than exit. Departing from the United States’ episodic tradition of making temporary investments to facilitate emergency bailouts, this growing trend more closely resembles state capitalism abroad. 

Arising from regulatory authority rather than voting rights, the government’s coercive power over a corporate board exceeds that of any private shareholder. This sovereign influence produces sovereign deference when the board prioritizes the government’s policy agenda over all investors’ financial returns. Deference is synergistic when the government provides the corporation with commensurate value but extractive when it does not. Though no public record yet shows extractive deference at the government’s portfolio firms, this Article anticipates that risk.

Because its minority stakes fall below Delaware’s new statutory thresholds for shareholder control, the government is a controller in fact but not in law. Accordingly, extractive deference would generally avoid judicial review, even though the traditional rationale for scrutinizing controller transactions is fully present. The government thus enjoys a controller’s coercive power without the legal safeguards that are supposed to check it.

The paradox presented by sovereign equity reveals a mismatch between state corporate law and the new federal investment program. While countries with histories of state shareholding have enacted specialized laws, Delaware treats the government like any other shareholder. 

Similarly, current transaction terms borrow inapt protections designed for ordinary investors. This Article proposes a contractual process of valuation and compensation, adapted from abroad, to address the causes and effects of extractive deference by constraining the board’s decision-making process rather than the government’s voting rights. Together with comprehensive public disclosures, this structure could better mitigate sovereign equity’s unique risks.

detail.abstract: India imports about nine-tenths of its crude, yet its supply-security debate often treats import risk as one quantity. We separate two failure modes: a physical one, in which cargoes cannot be obtained, and a cost one, in which crude is bought at a higher landed price, including the loss of the discount on Russian crude. First, the physical shock was largely converted into a price shock: Hormuz-locked suppliers delivered 12% of their October-2025 volumes in April-July 2026, yet India replaced about 5.8 million tonnes a month (28% of its import book) from suppliers outside the strait; refinery runs stayed within 1% of their October-2025 level while landed prices rose 59%. Second, the Russian discount, measured on landed prices, was worth about US$150 million a month in 2025 and became a premium in March-May 2026: the natural hedge is small and fails in the tail. Third, a filtered-historical-simulation model using information to October 2025 puts the one-month 97.5% expected shortfall of the import bill at US$1.1 billion; the March 2026 increase of US$7.0 billion lay beyond every simulated outcome. Resilience rested partly on Russian barrels made available by US sanctions policy, which couples the two modes. Filling the empty strategic caverns is the cheapest physical protection; reserves beat proactive diversification for disruptions shorter than about six months (3.5 if Russian supply is also blocked); and hedges should be sized to stressed landed exposure.

detail.abstract: Drone technology has evolved from remote-controlled aircraft into intelligent robotic systems integrating artificial intelligence, computer vision, autonomous navigation, advanced materials, wireless communication, and energy management. Recent patent-related developments highlight innovation beyond conventional flying machines, including morphing drones, intelligent payload interfaces, laser-based motion prediction, wireless energy sharing, and emergency recovery mechanisms. This article presents a qualitative review of selected drone-related patent developments reported during September-October 2026 and a broader dataset of patent records covering propulsion, battery systems, delivery infrastructure, autonomous inspection, environmental monitoring, marine robotics, swarm coordination, fire suppression, and cybersecurity. Particular attention is given to the technical principles, potential applications, limitations, and research opportunities associated with these inventions. The review also explains patent classifications, publication and grant status, patentfamily identification, and the importance of independent technical verification. It identifies research opportunities for students in energy-efficient navigation, uncertainty-aware sensing, modular payload systems, battery monitoring, infrastructure inspection, and multi-drone simulation. The findings indicate that future drone innovation will depend on integrating adaptive structures, intelligent sensing, reliable communication, efficient energy systems, and safety-conscious autonomous decision-making. Patent analysis offers a useful framework for identifying emerging engineering challenges, provided that published proposals are distinguished from validated technologies and commercially deployed products.

detail.abstract: Does technology denial work? The question is old and the answer has always split. We argue that the split reflects the level at which evidence is gathered: controls are written for a product, a process step and an end user, but judged by country, industry and year. Reconstructing China's semiconductor record for 2017–2026 from public and audited sources alone — the geographic revenue notes of sixty-three firms, customs returns at the eight-digit line by origin, two memory makers' 2026 prospectuses, the sanctions registers — we find that one control regime produced four responses, and that each follows from whether the input the rule reached could be replaced. Huawei, cut off from a frontier foundry, lost 42 percent of revenue against peers and half of its consumer business against its own carrier segment. Its home market recovered only when a domestic processor returned; its overseas market did not. Lithography imports rose fivefold with no domestic substitute. China's etch and deposition makers kept growing at 30–40 percent a year while foreign peers stalled, yet never exceeded their own pre-control trend: the controls shielded the covered segments from a downturn, at a cost carried by state capital. Bilateral trade statistics show at most a faint trace of the controls, and one that changes with the customs source consulted; the accounts of the toolmakers the controls named show a clear cycle in their China sales. Listing a firm did nothing; withholding an input did. Leakage is a property of legal chokepoints, not a failure of enforcement — and evidence is relevant by its place in the value chain, not by the discipline that filed it.

detail.abstract: AI computing power is rented by the hour, and futures on rental prices are about to trade. Yet compute cannot be stored, capacity takes years to build, and each chip generation is quickly replaced. This paper develops an equilibrium model of the risk premium on compute futures. Its central observation is that the steep rise in rental prices when capacity is tight is mostly a scarcity rent: a transfer from AI labs to compute providers, not a cost. A transfer cancels when both sides hedge it equally, so the sign of the premium depends on who participates in the futures market. Futures trade below expected rental prices if and only if providers' participation relative to labs' exceeds a threshold, which rises with real congestion costs and with right skew in demand. With two demand states, this condition holds for any risk-averse preferences. Along the futures curve, most of the slope is expected depreciation, and the premium can change sign across maturities. A futures market raises capacity when the market is tight but can lower it when capacity is slack. Calibrated to public rental-price data, the model implies that the positive premium in early evidence requires providers to hedge at least about 56-58% as much as labs.

detail.abstract: When is a price just? This paper develops a new theory of justice in pricing, grounded in the Austrian market process tradition. Prices, I argue, are not merely outcomes to be evaluated against an external standard of fairness. They are instruments through which the competitive process performs morally significant functions: communicating information, generating incentives and coordinating the plans of millions under pervasive ignorance. When this process is operating, the prices it produces carry a genuine presumption of justice. I establish this claim through two complementary arguments and demonstrate its power across cases from price gouging to wages to monopoly.

detail.abstract: Economics has long split its assumption about human motivation into two poles. The rationalagent tradition compresses all motives into a single utility function, in which stratification is invisible; behavioral economics decomposes motives into a list of biases, which is fragmented and unstructured. Psychology offers stratified schemes, but lacks an interface to economic behavior. This paper proposes an ontological reconstruction of the desiring person: desire is not a lump but a stratified structure with a generative architecture. Six layers of desire are generated by three domains and two directions: the resource domain generates the preservation layer and the gambling layer; the social domain generates the emotional-belonging layer and the esteem layer; the transcendence domain generates the growth layer and the meaning-altruism layer. The two directions across the three domains unify into a single polarity axis, preservation versus pursuit. The generative thread is the desire radius, expanding outward from mine, to yours, to the world; the six layers are the product structure of three distance circles times two polarities. Each layer is an information decoder: the same information is decoded into different signals by different layers, and information passing through a person is decoded by the six layers into a signal matrix. The paper offers three foundations (developmental psychology, linguistics, and the genealogy of autonomy), a two-question criterion for a closure check of the layer count, four principles of priority decoding, and three falsifiable discriminating predictions. Unlike Maslow's staircase, the six layers here are triggered in parallel rather than satisfied sequentially. The paper upgrades desire stratification from ad hoc enumeration to structural generation, providing a microfoundation for the group heterogeneity of policy effects.

detail.abstract: Researchers decomposing stock market returns into cash-flow and discount-rate news with a vector autoregression (VAR) face a dilemma. The VAR cannot be estimated precisely with many predictors as state variables; with few, its news estimates depend on which are chosen. We escape this dilemma by sorting 25 predictors into three groups by persistence and using each group's forecast combination as a state variable. A VAR that recovers true news must produce discount-rate news that forecasts returns and cash-flow news that forecasts dividend growth, with neither adding to the other's forecast. Ours does, and its estimates are stable across design choices.

detail.abstract: Groups, not just individuals, carry out search over candidates, products, and projects, yet standard approaches treat search as an individual activity. In laboratory experiments, we study groups that sequentially sample alternatives, varying stopping-decision rules and the alignment of group members' preferences, and compare them to individuals under identical conditions. Individuals undersearch, lowering their standards over time; groups with aligned preferences instead set higher, more consistent standards and reject low-value alternatives more often, closing the gap with optimal search predictions-especially under stricter stopping rules-and raising welfare. With misaligned preferences, collective search backfires: high-value alternatives are rejected more often because agreement is harder to reach, even though participants lower their standards. The paper thus identifies sequential exploration as a novel mechanism behind why groups outperform or underperform individuals, challenging approaches that treat group search as if a single "unitary" decision maker were at work.

detail.abstract: How do governmental organizations accumulate institutional knowledge despite recurrent political change? Existing research has explained long-term political development through concepts such as Critical Junctures and path dependence, yet has devoted comparatively less attention to the organizational conditions under which institutional learning becomes possible. This paper develops a deductive framework linking four latent theoretical constructs-organizational continuity, organizational knowledge accumulation, institutional learning, and Protective Belts-to their observable empirical implications. Political Frameworks are introduced as historically grounded environments generated by successive Critical Junctures, while Protective Belts are conceptualized as organization-specific constraint structures that selectively preserve organizational continuity within the same historical environment. Because these theoretical constructs are not directly observable, the empirical analyses employ ministerial duration as an indicator of the conditions under which organizational knowledge may accumulate. The framework is evaluated using an original dataset of 1,062 ministerial spells covering five governmental organizations in Peru between 1821 and 2026. Kaplan-Meier estimates and Cox proportional hazards models provide qualified support for the theoretical propositions. Political Frameworks explain important historical differences in ministerial continuity but do not generate a monotonic historical progression. Within the post-1993 Political Framework, the Ministry of Economy and Finance exhibits comparatively greater organizational continuity following the consolidation of Peru's macroeconomic governance, consistent with the proposed role of Protective Belts. Beyond the Peruvian case, the paper contributes a deductive framework that integrates comparative-historical institutionalism and organizational theory by distinguishing historical environments from the organizational mechanisms through which institutional learning develops.

detail.abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical machine learning is increasingly tested in financial settings, yet evaluations rarely make it possible to attribute observed behavior to the quantum components themselves. We study one concrete decision problem: choosing a binary portfolio allocation under a budget constraint, where the risk term is estimated from generated joint credit-spread stress scenarios. We build a modular pipeline, SynQubi, with two quantum components in isolated, swappable roles: a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) that generates tail scenarios, benchmarked against empirical, Gaussian, and Student-𝑡 copulas, and a QAOA optimizer, whose proposals are certified against exact classical solvers. Across seeds, on non-degenerate instances QAOA matches classical references on solution quality but is markedly worse on constraint satisfaction, returning budget-feasible allocations in roughly half of samples against the null model's all. Our main finding is methodological: certification overturned five of our own results that ordinary inspection had passed, and the errors pointed in different directions (two flattered the quantum components, three did not). Such errors cannot be fixed by discounting favorable results, only by a mechanical classical reference. A small pilot on LLM-generated trading-strategy code shows the same pattern in an LLM setting: a harness of mechanical validity checks found that every failure was a missing import, not a misunderstanding of the strategy. We establish no quantum advantage. CCS Concepts • Computing methodologies → Intelligent agents; • Applied computing → Economics.

detail.abstract: The prospect of Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) is frequently framed as a competition between human and machine intelligence. This article argues that such framing rests on an analytically restrictive conception of intelligence as a property of individual agents. It develops the concept of GCI as an open, distributed, multi-level, and historically evolving sociotechnical system through which individuals, groups, institutions, cultures, technologies, and collective memory participate in the generation, validation, interpretation, transmission, and institutionalization of knowledge, values, and adaptive strategies. The article distinguishes computational intelligence from civilizational intelligence and argues that superior performance in computationally formalizable tasks does not, by itself, establish superiority over a civilization-scale system. It further separates epistemic novelty from normative agency and goal generation from goal legitimation. On this basis, the article proposes a two-level model of Civilizational Alignment comprising (1) intra-GCI processes for representing and legitimating plural values and (2) GCI-ASI mechanisms for aligning advanced AI capabilities with legitimate institutional objectives constraints and accountability arrangements. The article introduces Epistemic Closure Risk as a theoretical construct concerning the possible homogenization of knowledge ecosystems under excessive dependence on recursively generated synthetic information, while explicitly distinguishing this hypothesis from the empirically established phenomenon of Model Collapse. A multi-capital governance framework is then proposed to evaluate civilization-scale AI decisions across human, social/institutional, natural, cultural, intellectual/epistemic, and economic capital. Six theoretical propositions and a research agenda for operationalizing GCI, human-AI complementarity epistemic diversity and Civilizational Alignment are developed. The principal contribution is to shift the theoretical question from whether ASI will become "smarter than humanity" toward the institutional and epistemic architecture required for a civilization to incorporate an artificial cognitive component of potentially far greater computational capacity without surrendering pluralism, accountability, epistemic diversity, and collective selfdetermination.

detail.abstract: We develop a new individual difference measure of spending attitudes, specifically the distinction between "tightwads" who find it painful to spend money (and, as a result, underspend) and "spendthrifts" who spend freely (and overspend). The original Spendthrift-Tightwad (ST-TW) scale (Rick et al., 2008) measured this trait with a small number of heterogeneous items that included the tightwad and spendthrift labels themselves, and had other weaknesses. detail.abstract: The CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) is widely treated as a gauge of market risk, yet it measures only the market's expected volatility over roughly the next 30 days, as implied by S&P 500 option prices. This paper argues that such a measure gives an incomplete picture of systemic risk, because structural vulnerabilities can build during calm periods without appearing in option prices. Drawing on Minsky's Financial Instability Hypothesis, Kownatzki's evidence on the VIX, Adrian and Brunnermeier's CoVaR, and research on margin spirals and short-seller behavior, it proposes Latent Stability Risk (LSR), a conceptual framework organized around three channels of hidden fragility: leverage accumulation, short-seller retreat, and liquidity overconfidence. A qualitative look at 2006-2008 illustrates how the channels fit a known crisis. LSR is intended to complement the VIX, not replace it, and it has not been tested. It is a proposal for future empirical work, not a validated measure or prediction tool.

detail.abstract: This paper develops laboratory panarchism as an account of the institutional structure and learning processes of overlapping governance systems, where at least some jurisdictions follow persons, functions, contracts, or affiliations. Its philosophical premise is fallibilist: no authority can know in advance which rule bundle will work across heterogeneous circumstances. Its practical premise is constitutional: rules of membership, jurisdiction, interoperability, and revision shape whether comparative experience becomes observable and actionable. Laboratory panarchism has two levels. Clubs, functional jurisdictions, cultural autonomies, and digitally native organisations are first-order laboratories. The wider order is a secondorder laboratory in which these systems compete, cooperate, interfere, exchange members, transmit practices, and revise their common interfaces. Territorial and non-territorial arrangements can coexist within this order; learning can concern their rules and which functions remain bundled together. Overlapping membership supports a mechanism-interpersonal constitutional discovery-because differently governed people can compare rules through ordinary relations and carry practices between organisations without necessarily moving residence. The theory separates exposure from learning, learning from actionability, and first-order adaptation from revision of system-wide metarules. It extends laboratory federalism, club theory, polycentric governance, and policy-diffusion research rather than presuming that greater institutional variety is beneficial. I formulate six observable propositions and specify conditions under which overlap instead produces lock-in, biased comparison, cost displacement, capture, fragmentation, or institutional overload. The claim is positive and comparative: non-territoriality matters when it changes who encounters institutional alternatives, how knowledge travels, which response margins are available, and whether governance organisations can act on what their members learn.

detail.abstract: Oversight and transparency regimes in corporate law share a common architecture: they require that information systems exist, that senior officers certify what those systems produce, and that boards respond when signals reach them. This article asks why institutions that satisfy this architecture nonetheless fail, and what a literary case of institutional failure adds to the legal analysis. Using doctrinal and comparative methods, it examines Delaware's Caremark line (including Marchand v. Barnhill and In re McDonald's), the Sarbanes-Oxley certification regime, Brazil's Lei das Sociedades por Ações and CVM enforcement, and the UK Corporate Governance Code's Provision 29, with the Enron/Arthur Andersen and Americanas matters as institutional illustrations. The Brazilian novel O Prédio que Aprendeu a Escutar, in which a São Paulo courthouse's case system begins issuing unauthored, uncontestable entries that certify employees' private suffering, is used not as evidence but as a heuristic case that isolates the step at which a signal becomes an institutionally valid record. The article argues that the doctrines examined test whether a reporting channel exists and whether signals reach the board, but rarely ask whether the resulting record remained contestable, by someone with independent access to the underlying facts, before it became final. This contestability gap helps explain why failures can cluster where procedural compliance is high and verification is internal, and it is sharpest for human-capital and psychosocial risks that lack a financial-statement anchor. The article proposes a modest four-question interpretive test, outlines limited regulatory implications, addresses the strongest objections, and states conditions that would falsify the thesis. The analysis is doctrinal and interpretive rather than empirical, and its conclusions are qualified accordingly.

detail.abstract: In January 2025, the United Kingdom applied 20% VAT to private school fees, ending an exemption in place since 1973. Using England's annual school census, we track birth cohorts across local authorities and estimate how progression from one age to the next within the independent sector changed at each stage of schooling. Because the tax applied everywhere at once, identification rests on a within-sector contrast between transition and continuing ages in the same authority and year, tested against alternative trends and placebo estimates. By January 2026, progression into independent sixth forms had fallen by 11 log points relative to continuing cohorts, and to the pre-reform differential; after adjusting for the historical linear trend, it was 7 log points, still outside the range of placebo estimates. Entry to secondary school at 11 shows no detectable change, and enrolled cohorts thinned by only 1 to 4 log points at other ages (1 to 2.6 at ages 11 to 15). Most of the decline in mainstream independent enrolment was concentrated within continuing schools, while register exits were not unusually high relative to historical reports, although definitions are not directly comparable. The concentration of the response at the sixth-form transition is consistent with lower switching costs and greater availability of alternatives at that stage, and suggests that, if the pattern persists, the aggregate effect of the tax will build as successive cohorts reach that margin.

detail.abstract: Generative models of option surfaces now construct risk-neutral measures by projecting a learned physical generator onto option prices. A premium recovered in this way can be produced by the surface representation, by the finite sample of the projection or by the generator itself. We build an audit that separates these sources. It combines a discretized, completely affine Heston oracle with a known pathwise pricing kernel, independent Monte Carlo clouds for fitting, normalizing and auditing the projection, a sequential accounting of the squared premium error across identification, representation, systematic generator, training and Monte Carlo layers, and a test of the implied oneday pricing kernel on realized returns of SPX option contracts excluded from the projection book, reported together with its power. Representation contamination is large in entropy but confined to nearly hedged directions, and the finite-sample entropy floor 𝑟/(2𝑁) holds from 5,000 draws per cloud. In this benchmark the binding error is the generator's conditional mean of the one-day return. A conditional latent diffusion that beats an AR(1) forecast misses a true premium of about 1.6 bp by 20 to 29 bp on every training seed, while a DYSANOS-style generator that forecasts worse comes within 2 bp of it once Monte Carlo noise is removed. Re-centring the diffusion's own draws on a one-parameter return drift lowers its squared premium error by a factor of 15 to 34 and recovers the level of the premium but not its daily variation. On SPX, in exploratory analyses of a test period that an earlier run had already used, no learned kernel satisfies the Stage I joint diagnostic criteria fixed before the final exploratory run, and with all quotes included only the tests in the calm volatility regime have the power to reject a kernel at the size of the observed option premia.

detail.abstract: Generative AI raises a worker's output today and reduces the learning that comes from doing the work herself. It also changes what output reveals: employers who cannot see skill infer it from output, and AI raises output without raising skill. This paper studies how much work workers leave to AI in a labour market with search frictions, turnover, incentive pay and employer learning about skill. When the market can see skill, it prices skill at its social value, so the trade-off between output and learning is resolved efficiently: neither AI, nor lost learning, nor employer learning is by itself a source of inefficiency. When skill must be inferred, a single object governs the inefficiency: Ω, the value of the market's beliefs that leaks out of the current employment relationship when the worker moves. Hidden learning is undervalued by exactly Ω, and output produced by AI is read as skill with weight proportional to Ω. Coordination between the worker and her current employer cannot reach Ω, because it accrues to employers she has not yet met. The market therefore adopts AI on learning tasks at a lower AI capability than is efficient. Over-use rises with turnover and falls with AI-proof assessment, with performance pay, and with the information about skill that job changes reveal. Because AI's productivity gain varies across tasks in ways employers cannot see, AI also makes output a noisier signal of skill and slows employer learning. In a calibration to junior workers in which job changes reveal little about skill, entrants leave a fifth of their work to AI when the efficient share is zero, and skill after ten years is lower by 6.7% of entry output. The magnitude falls quickly as job changes reveal more, but over-use persists whenever AI's gain for novices lies between the market's and the planner's adoption thresholds. The distortion is concentrated at labour-market entry and is driven by junior turnover combined with fast learning and large AI gains for novices, not by employers knowing little about juniors. Ongoing AI-proof assessment, net of its cost, closes most of the welfare loss; an entry credential does not help.

detail.abstract: A lender who cannot observe how a household will pay prices its risk at the average of its score tranche, and the household pays that average for the life of the contract. This paper argues that when observing and verifying conduct becomes cheap enough, and conduct carries predictive information beyond the score, contracts that update the risk premium explicitly and share the gains from that information with the borrower become viable — and writes one down. In a 36-month rent-to-own contract operating in Chile, every payment is a bank transfer recorded in an immutable ledger, and the risk premium is reviewed yearly on a declared rule and can only fall. We propose a hierarchical Bayesian model, anchored on the bureau PD, that turns a household's payment history into its own predictive PD, and prove four results: each clean month lowers the PD; the clean history is the envelope, so the largest reduction at each review is finite and computable but depends on a dispersion that payments alone do not identify; payments identify the event's mean and dispersion but not its link to default; and, for a rare event with its link and dispersion held fixed, learning speed is approximately proportional to its frequency. On a worked contract the installment falls from 34.83 to 34.59 UF after one clean year. The contract exists for the discipline that a transparent, conduct-contingent price induces; we state its self-financing condition, pre-register the protocol, and compute the sample sizes at which each hypothesis becomes testable.

detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative AI coding assistants such as Claude, GitHub Copilot, and Cursor has changed how software is produced, but not obviously why it is difficult to deliver. This article presents a narrative, practice-oriented synthesis of the recurring problems faced by full stack developers across the frontend (React and Angular), the backend (Java and Spring Boot), the data tier, and production delivery on AWS and Azure. It asks which problems recur, where and why they concentrate, and how AI-assisted development changes the skills, workflows, and governance needed to address them. It argues that these problems concentrate at the boundaries between layers, teams, and environments and at scale: cross-layer debugging, API contracts, data consistency, security, observability, and operational ownership. Faster code generation does not remove them. The evidence on AI assistance is mixed. A controlled experiment found developers about 55.8% faster on a scoped task, a randomized trial of experienced maintainers in mature codebases found completion time rose by about 19%, and an analysis of early Copilot output found that approximately 40% of programs generated for security-relevant scenarios were vulnerable. A large practitioner survey shows widespread adoption alongside limited trust in the accuracy of AI output. The article therefore contends that AI raises the premium on fundamentals, system design, verification, security reasoning, and operational accountability. Its contributions are an analytical framework of ten recurring challenges; a heuristic for deciding when to rely on AI assistance; a seven-step verification workflow and review rubric for AI-generated code; end-to-end flow models for the frontend, authentication, backend, release, runtime, and incident response; a production-oriented treatment of DevOps and cloud deployment; a worked example of an idempotent payment submission across three layers; and implications for developers and engineering managers, with particular attention to regulated financial services. The study is a narrative synthesis, not a systematic review. Its examples and heuristics are illustrative and have not been validated empirically, and the cited studies differ in population, task, and tooling and should not be pooled. Its guidance is best treated as a set of hypotheses to test in an organization's own context.

We build a calibrated search model in which renewable, employment-contingent maternity benefits give parity-one employment option value: one-child mothers lower reservation wages and accept lower-quality jobs. detail.abstract: This paper proposes the foundational design principles for a non-technical cyber threat intelligence (CTI) information sharing framework aimed at critical infrastructure industries. While technical standards for CTI have matured, organizational reluctance to share persists due to social and economic friction like transaction costs, reputational risk, and legal liabilities such as Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs). To address this, the author models CTI sharing using both non-cooperative game theory (a duopoly Prisoner's Dilemma and a dynamic breach-reporting game) and empirical case studies (ViaSat/AcidRain and FireEye/SolarWinds). As a solution, the paper shifts to a cooperative game theory approach centered on Grand Coalition Bargaining. It proposes utilizing a dynamic and equitable distribution mechanism (such as the Shapley value) to ensure coalition stability, alongside public policy interventions like government-provided, tiered cyberinsurance to eliminate information asymmetry and incentivize robust CTI collaboration.

detail.abstract: Meeting the Paris Agreement target and path (PTP) is vital to protect humanity from the worse impacts of global warming. Using a large dimensional and unique Global Trade Analysis Project (GTAP) model for energy and international trade, we calculated the needed change in the energy mix and fall in carbon emissions to meet a minimal PTP of less than 2 o C warming. Covering 30 countries/regions and 31 commodity sectors, the model shows the PTP in annual time steps to 2100 in terms of emissions reduction and the shift in energy mix allowing for changes in energy intensity, renewables growth, and rising carbon prices. By 2050, using a year 2019 baseline, model results show carbon emissions must decrease on a compound basis by at least 5.7% globally, per year, on average, and coal consumption must fall continuously from 2025, complemented by large increases in renewable energy that allow for continued economic growth. Coal consumption must decline between 85-99% by 2050 among the key emitters (China, the USA, and India), compared to 2019 (the model baseline), complemented by a continuous transition to renewables. For Net-Zero Emissions Targets (NZET), carbon sequestration, such as from reforestation and land use change, is also essential, although with substantial uncertainty. Model results indicate a net-zero outcome, even with assumed carbon sequestration, occurs no earlier than 2058, at best.

detail.abstract: U.S. charitable food networks distribute billions of dollars in publicly funded food assistance through food banks, pantries and meal programs, many of them faith-based and volunteer-run. Yet the system has historically measured success mainly by pounds distributed and people served. In 2024, the Government Accountability Office found that USDA has no performance assessment system or measurable goals for The Emergency Food Assistance Program (TEFAP) and the Commodity Supplemental Food Program (CSFP), and in 2025 USDA terminated its annual national food security report. The sector has made real progress, including Feeding America's Service Insights platform and its Network Measurement, Evaluation and Learning approach, but gaps remain in the coverage, funding and implementation of common, outcome-level measurement, particularly among smaller community and faith-based organizations. This paper argues that charitable food networks can narrow these gaps by adapting accountability practices long required in U.S.-funded international food assistance: documented indicator reference sheets, data quality assessments, post-distribution monitoring, participant feedback and complaints mechanisms, and structured learning reviews. It proposes a tiered monitoring, evaluation, accountability and learning (MEAL) model designed for volunteer-run affiliates, a sample core indicator set, and recommendations for networks, funders and state TEFAP agencies. The model measures contribution to results rather than claiming impact.

detail.abstract: Digital transformation has changed what human resource management can measure, and with it the expectation that the HR function should contribute to organizational performance on the strength of evidence rather than intuition. HR analytics-the systematic use of workforce data and statistical analysis to inform people decisions-sits at the center of this shift. This paper reviews the conceptual and empirical literature published through 2019 to assess how, and under what conditions, HR analytics improves organizational performance. It argues that analytics does not create value automatically by virtue of better data or more sophisticated tools; value emerges only when analytical work is connected to a business question, translated into a decision, and acted upon. Drawing on evidence-based reviews and case studies, the paper distinguishes descriptive reporting from genuinely predictive and prescriptive analytics, and it identifies a persistent gap between the promise of HR analytics and its realized impact. The paper develops a capability-based account in which the performance payoff from analytics depends on four complementary assets: data infrastructure, analytical skill, the credibility to influence decisions, and a culture that treats evidence as legitimate grounds for action. It locates the most common failure modes-metrics disconnected from strategy, analysis that never reaches a decision-maker, and technical capability unsupported by business understanding-and it draws implications for how HR functions can build analytics capacity that actually moves organizational outcomes. To render the capability concrete, the paper advances a proposed explainable and causal analytics framework for employee attrition that not only predicts who is likely to leave, using gradient-boosted trees, random forests, and neural networks, but explains why, through model-agnostic attribution, and estimates which retention interventions would actually reduce risk, through causal machine learning and counterfactual reasoning. An illustrative evaluation is reported to demonstrate the protocol and is clearly labeled as hypothetical pending empirical validation. The paper concludes that HR analytics is best understood not as a technology to be purchased but as an organizational capability to be built, and that the value of a predictive model is realized only when it is made explainable, causal, and tied to an intervention.

detail.abstract: Legal benchmarks of large language models (LLMs) commonly report a "hallucination rate". A widely cited operationalisation, by Magesh et al. (2025), decomposes factual hallucination into correctness and groundedness and labels a response as hallucinated when it is incorrect or misgrounded. This paper argues, on the basis of a working benchmark of LLMs on Polish civil procedure (LexAlpha Lab), that the framework does not apply to civil-law systems without modification. Three observations support the claim: (1) the two dimensions overlap on the error types that matter most in statute-based law; (2) a wrong case citation and incorrect content attributed to a statutory provision do not carry the same weight where the statute, not the judgment, is the source of law; (3) the currency of the provision's wording, which Polish official sources (ISAP) date precisely, is not measured by any of the empirical benchmarks reviewed here. I propose to replace the binary question "did the model hallucinate?" with "is the answer correctly grounded?", defined as: the cited designation exists, the source supports the content attributed to it, and the wording was in force on the legal-state date of the question. Preliminary results from 65 answers (10 models without tools, 3 systems with search; 4 model judges, Cohen's κ 0.81–0.93 against the cards before the author's review) are reported, together with the limitations of the pilot and the reasons for keeping the criteria simple enough to re-run on every monthly model release. Version 1.2 adds a test of the model judges on cards closed before any judge ran: the judges, all with web search, are accurate on errors that can be detected with the answer, the answer key and the scoring rules, and inaccurate on errors that require a source which web search does not reliably return (stale wording, a real case number attached to a thesis from another case). A verification report produced from the official sources by citation-checking code and a model-based support check, given to the judge as auxiliary evidence raised the agreement of one judge with the lawyer's cards (Sol 6.1, κ 0.84 → 0.97) and lowered that of another (Gemini 4 Argon, κ 0.95 → 0.88); the same report used as binding evidence lowered the agreement of both. A third variant, which shows a verification status instead of "✓" whenever the wording on the legal-state date was not established, left the agreement of one judge unchanged and lowered that of the other relative to the second variant.

detail.abstract: Tackling poverty calls for more than an assessment of whether incomes are adequate. Human development strategies are therefore pertinent to poverty reduction, since they widen the evidence base on poverty by examining how people are deprived of their functionings and capabilities. The Human Development Index (HDI) of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) is widely regarded as the most comprehensive measure available, yet it neither fully fits nor adequately captures human development as understood in Islam. Drawing on the five objectives of Maqasid Sharī'ah, namely the protection of religion (Ad-Din), life (An-Nafs), intellect (Al-Aql), progeny (Al-Nasl) and wealth (Al-Mal), the study builds an Islamic Human Development Index (i-HDI). It then combines index construction with panel regression to examine how the i-HDI relates to poverty reduction. The findings indicate that the Islamic components of human development matter significantly for reducing poverty and offer a workable alternative to the HDI. The study thus deepens understanding of the poverty problem and supports the design of better-targeted policies and plans, particularly for member states of the OIC.

detail.abstract: Repeated banking and financial crises have exposed how complex and fragile the conventional financial and banking system can be. This paper provides empirical evidence on how environmental, social and governance (ESG) disclosure affects banking stability, and on how each ESG pillar contributes to that effect, paying special attention to the moderating role of capital structure. The analysis draws on a combined panel of 17 Islamic and 25 conventional banks from the MENA region, Indonesia and Malaysia observed between 2014 and 2022, estimated with random-effects and GMM panel models. The findings show that the overall ESG score exerts a positive and significant influence on banking stability. When the score is broken down into its pillars, only environmental and governance practices are significantly and positively associated with stability, whereas the social pillar shows no significant effect. Islamic banks are consistently more stable than their conventional counterparts, a result that is in keeping with the ethical foundations of Islamic finance. Moreover, the stability of both Islamic and conventional banks is driven chiefly by capital structure, particularly equity adequacy, and by the management of credit risk. By documenting the central role of capital structure in moderating the gains from ESG disclosure, the study addresses an effect that earlier research has largely left unexplored.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a value-theory framework that uses time as a common unit of measurement, aiming to reconcile the long-standing opposition between subjective and objective theories of value. The core proposition is that actors do not directly compare subjective utility with objective costs when making decisions; rather, they convert both into time costs for estimation. Monetary price P is transformed into indirect time cost P/w through the wage rate w, while direct time costs (such as search time and waiting time) are measured directly in time units. Whether an action actually occurs depends on the constraint U >= t_total: subjective utility evaluation must be no less than the total time cost. This paper further advances the proposition that "price precedes value": the initial price is not a monetary expression of intrinsic value, but the starting point of the market's discovery of value; the buyer's value judgment is activated only after the price appears; subjective evaluation is transformed into market price signals through objective data such as transaction volume; and price movements constitute a dynamic process of continuous interaction between suppliers and buyers.

detail.abstract:
Classical neoclassical finance, rooted in the Efficient Market Hypothesis (Fama, 1970) and continuous geometric Brownian motion (Samuelson, 1965), assumes asset prices follow frictionless, memoryless random walks driven by exogenous information arrivals. However, institutional execution reality and empirical high-frequency market microstructure reveal that price formation is fundamentally a discrete, dissipative thermodynamic process: algorithmic capital order flow performs directional mechanical work against a non-linear spatial resistance field constituted by resting limit order books and historically trapped inventory.

This paper establishes the First-Principles Market Mechanics (FPMM) framework. We formalize an equity asset as a constrained discrete mass particle governed by a Langevin-type stochastic differential equation traversing a one-dimensional scalar gravitational potential field. Net institutional capital inflow is mapped to external mechanical work W = ∫ F_ext dx, while the historical Volume-at-Price Profile (VPP)—modulated by an exponential temporal memory-decay kernel w(τ) = λ^τ with λ ∈ (0, 1)—is mapped to an overhead resistance density functional RD(x) and a dimensionless potential coordinate Φ ∈ [0, 1]. We derive the multiplicative dynamic critical turnover envelope FT_max(Φ) and the regularized intraday barycentric propulsion deviation ratio (VWAP_PDE), rigorously proving the boundedness, orthogonality, and completeness of seven discrete thermodynamic and kinematic phase regimes.

Empirical cross-sectional and longitudinal out-of-sample evaluations across the S&P 100 universe from 2020 to 2026 demonstrate that FPMM eliminates heuristic technical indicator lag, resolves false-breakout whipsaws, and achieves a statistically significant improvement in regime-conditional Sharpe ratio (t-stat = 4.82) while pre-identifying high-altitude gravitational collapses prior to liquidity cascades.

detail.abstract: The vision of Viksit Bharat 2047 requires an innovation ecosystem that enables students to transform knowledge, creativity, and scientific thinking into practical solutions for economic development and public welfare. detail.abstract: Which commodities can share an input reporting group when the objective is to evaluate a fixed policy? We study local tax welfare with known demand responses and common CES production substitution, but unknown product input assignments consistent with group accounts. Unless parent information already identifies welfare, products can remain together exactly when their proportional policy loads agree and their adjusted demand responses differ only by terms canceled by known resource balances. This rule determines a unique coarsest successful classification. With nested CES demand and nest-uniform proportional tax directions, pooling within a nest requires conditional substitution to match production substitution. An untaxed nest can require finer reporting than a taxed nest. Exact guarantees generically require singleton reporting, so we also study positive tolerances. In a structured two-factor class, diffuse sales leave a positive limiting welfare width under every coarse classification; concentrated sales can make a small refinement sufficient. An input second moment can recover what group totals omit. The results identify when to pool, when to refine, and when a different report can supply the required precision. detail.abstract:
Mexico’s extensive participation in international manufacturing and trade networks has coexisted with weak growth in income per person and limited institutional inclusion. This paper examines that development paradox through the Economics of Belonging, distinguishing five objectives: growth, stability, distribution, human capabilities, and social and institutional belonging. It uses audited analytical files for a purposive 55-country sample and compares Mexico with Latin American peers, the United States, South Korea, China, Spain, and the United Kingdom.

Mexico’s average annual real GDP per capita growth was 0.49% during 2000–2019. Its 2023 Human Development Index was 0.789, while its constructed institutional-access score was 36.9 out of 100. Perceived governmental care, at 59.3%, presents a more favorable regional comparison, revealing an asymmetry between institutional access and perceived recognition.

A detailed comparison with South Korea documents substantially different development trajectories: real GDP per capita multiplied approximately 2.47 times in Mexico and 35.03 times in Korea between 1960 and 2023. The paper examines domestic saving, investment, industrial coordination, and capability formation as mechanisms connecting access to international demand with domestic productivity and widely shared income gains. It also considers how relational support may buffer weak economic performance while becoming vulnerable to persistent exclusion.

The analysis distinguishes descriptive associations from causal identification and formulates testable propositions concerning domestic supplier linkages, capability gaps, institutional access, and the durability of perceived governmental care. External integration is assessed through the domestic opportunities and institutional relations it enables, rather than treated as a sufficient indicator of development.

detail.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted technique for knowledge transfer, in which a teacher model guides the training of a student model. However, conventional KD methods assume that the teacher's predictions are reliable, while in practice teacher models may produce incorrect outputs.To address this limitation, we propose Corrective Knowledge Distillation (CTKD), a framework that introduces teacher error identification and rectification into the distillation process.For classification tasks, we correct knowledge misalignment through probability calibration, where the maximum probability index is adjusted to align with the ground-truth label. For regression tasks with continuous targets, we design a reference-anchored correction strategy that selectively moves the teacher's dose prediction toward the reference dose in unreliable regions, weighting each correction by the agreement between the predicted dose gradient and anatomy.Experiments on multiple medical imaging tasks show that the proposed method improves selected evaluation metrics rather than every metric. For classification, CTKD improves accuracy by 0.31%, 1.97%, and 0.72% on four-class, three-class, and two-class tasks, respectively. For segmentation, CTKD achieves Dice improvements of 1.25% on KiTS19 (0.7885 vs. 0.7788) and 2.10% on LiTS17 (0.5096 vs. 0.4991). For regression, CTKD reduces Dose Difference from 9.246 to 8.788 on OpenKBP (-4.9%), while DVH Difference increases from 4.698 to 5.041, indicating a trade-off between global dose accuracy and dose-volume consistency.These results indicate that correcting teacher knowledge before transfer improves selected evaluation metrics in medical imaging tasks, with improvement dependent on the task.

detail.abstract: Recent advances in computational pathology have been propelled by multiple instance learning, which enables slide-level prediction without the need for exhaustive pixel-level annotations. However, standard multiple instance learning models suffer from catastrophic forgetting when new data or tasks emerge, requiring computationally expensive joint retraining to maintain performance. Although recent efforts have attempted to integrate class-incremental learning into the multiple instance learning framework, existing approaches are commonly evaluated under simplified settings with regular task structure and larger task increments. This does not fully reflect clinical reality, where new data and diagnostic categories arrive irregularly, even one at a time, under constraints that may preclude storing and replaying prior data. To address this, we introduce MonoCMIL, a continual learning framework tailored for mono-class incremental updates while preserving prior knowledge without retraining. Extensive experiments on 18 pathology datasets with 34 categories demonstrate that MonoCMIL achieves a superior stability-plasticity trade-off across various class-incremental settings, establishing a practical step toward real-world continual learning for computational pathology.

detail.abstract: Healthcare leaders already know the standard list of cybersecurity controls: multi-factor authentication, patching, strong passwords, firewalls, backups, training, encryption, access control, and audits. Yet healthcare has had the highest average breach cost of any industry for more than a decade, and ransomware now drives nearly half of healthcare breaches. This paper asks why a well-known list keeps failing in practice. It reviews three documented incidents, the 2017 WannaCry attack on England's National Health Service, the 2021 ransomware attack on United Health Centers of the San Joaquin Valley, and the 2024 Change Healthcare attack, and traces each to a control that was known but missing. It then tests nine core controls against the realities of patient care, asking for each what the evidence shows, what clinical friction stands in the way, and where federal guidance now stands. The analysis finds that the gap between checklist and practice is not mainly a knowledge gap. It is a context gap. Shared workstations, legacy medical devices, round-the-clock operations, third-party concentration, and the clinical priority on availability all push organizations toward partial implementation. The paper also corrects two widely repeated practices, forced 90-day password changes and complexity rules, against current NIST guidance. It closes with implications for boards, security leaders, clinical leaders, and policymakers, and argues that healthcare cybersecurity should be governed as a patientsafety discipline, not a technical checklist.

detail.abstract: Photograph-based deep-learning models of gingivitis are mostly validated against visual grading, not clinical examination. We tested whether home-care habits of patients with fixed orthodontic appliances form layers differing in bleeding measured by probing and scored from photographs, and quantified what such scoring misses. In a secondary cross-sectional analysis of a public dataset (148 patients, Hanoi, Vietnam; Sulcus Bleeding Index [SBI] for 28 teeth; nine habit items; 1319 photographs), latent class analysis defined layers, an ordinal DINOv2 network scored SBI ≥ 2 per photographed tooth in nested patient-level cross-validation, and tooth-level generalized estimating equations located arch differences; confirmatory analyses were pre-registered. Minimal, basic-adjunct and intensive layers emerged (n = 33, 60, 55; limited stability), with mean SBI 2.21, 1.51 and 0.75 (intensive - minimal -1.46, 95% confidence interval [CI] -1.72 to -0.82). The difference spanned every tooth type (odds ratios 0.07–0.11), mainly as fewer bleeding teeth (minimal 92%, intensive 50%). The network detected teeth with SBI ≥ 2 with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.795 (95% CI 0.760–0.827). Patient-mean scores correlated with SBI of the photographed teeth (Spearman's ρ = 0.68; 0.76 after within-fold standardization) and less with SBI of the unphotographed molars (ρ = 0.53, standardized). Three questions reproduced the layer (Cohen's κ = 0.79). In this sample, self-reported habits form a diligence gradient whose bleeding difference spans the arch and appears in photograph-based scores trained on probing. Such scores do not replace molar probing; three questions are a candidate chairside screen needing validation.

detail.abstract: Corporate safety reports can improve after the rules for evaluating evidence have changed, even when the underlying operation remains unchanged. This Article examines the authority to make such changes and the information directors need to oversee them. It distinguishes express acceptance of an identified risk from an evidentiary override that changes the basis for operational approval. The Challenger record supplies a historical account of how a demand for assurance became a demand that objecting engineers prove danger. Delaware's Clovis and Collis decisions bring the treatment of evidence within contemporary oversight doctrine, while the two Boeing decisions show the importance of examining the board's actual response to reported problems. Comparison with British, German, and Dutch law connects the preservation of that record to duties of diligence and the substantiation of control statements. The Article proposes an Evidentiary Baseline Register through which material amendments receive independent technical review before the revised assessment supports release. A paired comparison explains the amendment's effect, and unresolved objections remain available to the official authorized to decide. The procedure extends to automated recalibration and supplier changes through defined delegations and contractual terms. Adoption through corporate policies, regulatory undertakings, or insurance arrangements gives the record legal significance appropriate to each instrument and provides a basis for examining how technical assurance was obtained.
